title: Work Breakdown Structure
in30Seconds: A work breakdown structure, or WBS, organizes a project’s full included scope into a hierarchy of deliverable-oriented pieces. It starts with the whole intended result, then divides it into smaller results until the parts are manageable enough to plan. The 100-percent concept checks that the children of any parent cover all of that parent’s included work—neither leaving work out nor quietly adding work outside it. A WBS helps connect scope to later schedule planning, but it is not itself a calendar, task sequence, or staffing chart.
whyItMatters: Large projects become hard to discuss when they are described only as one broad goal. A WBS gives people a shared view of the results and component work that belong to that goal, so they can notice missing pieces, duplicated pieces, and requests that do not fit the current scope. It can support later estimating, scheduling, risk discussion, and tracking, without promising that the project will be on time or successful. Learning its boundaries matters as much as learning its structure: a WBS organizes scope; it does not decide who has authority or replace a schedule.
learningObjectives: Define a work breakdown structure as a hierarchical, deliverable-oriented decomposition of project scope.
Explain the 100-percent concept as a check on included work at every parent-child level.
Distinguish a WBS from a schedule, task list, and organizational chart.
Identify an appropriate work package in a short hypothetical WBS.
Analyze how a missing or extra WBS component affects scope and later schedule planning.

collegeVersion.heading: A WBS makes the whole scope visible in parts
collegeVersion.body:
A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a hierarchy that decomposes a project’s included scope into smaller, deliverable-oriented components. At the top is the whole project result. Beneath it are major deliverables or coherent portions of the result; beneath those are smaller components. The point is not to make a decorative tree. It is to create a shared account of what the project must produce and the component work needed to produce it. A WBS therefore begins with scope and deliverables, not with a person’s calendar or job title.

Deliverable-oriented means that the hierarchy emphasizes results, components, or recognizable portions of a result. For a hypothetical neighborhood festival, a top-level WBS might include participant experience, event information, site readiness, and project coordination. “Welcome area” can be a deliverable component; “install welcome sign at 9:00 a.m.” is an activity that may later appear in a schedule. The same project can be represented as an indented outline, a tree, or a table. No display format makes the underlying thinking correct by itself. The useful test is whether readers can understand how the smaller components relate to the whole intended scope.

A WBS is also not an organizational chart. An organizational chart groups people or units by reporting relationship. A WBS groups the project result and its components by scope. One component may involve several people, and one person may contribute to several components. Later planning can relate work packages to roles or responsibility, but those relationships answer a different question. Keeping the structures separate avoids assuming that every department label is a project deliverable.

collegeVersion.heading: The 100-percent concept checks coverage and boundaries
collegeVersion.body:
The 100-percent concept is a simple but demanding coverage test. For any parent element, the set of child elements should represent all of the included work for that parent. In the other direction, the children should not smuggle in work that lies beyond the parent. If the festival’s “event information” parent includes a public event page, on-site directional signs, and a participant information sheet, those children together should account for its included information work. If one required accessibility notice is absent, the parent is not fully represented. If a child adds a permanent citywide tourism campaign that is outside the festival project, the hierarchy has expanded the scope.

The word “100 percent” does not mean that a team can know every future detail with certainty, finish everything perfectly, or assign exactly one hundred hours. It names the logical relationship between a defined parent and its children. The relationship can be checked as understanding improves. A project may refine a broad future component later, especially when the work has uncertainty. When that happens, the team should make the changed understanding visible rather than pretending the original outline was complete. Whether and how a real organization approves change is outside this general lesson.

The rule applies at more than one level. Suppose “site readiness” is divided into venue layout and participant access. The venue-layout children should cover the layout component; participant-access children should cover the access component; together those two branches should cover the stated site-readiness parent. The rule helps reveal overlap too. If the same accessibility notice is counted in two branches without an intentional reason, later estimates or tracking can double-count it. It does not eliminate judgment, but it supplies a disciplined question: where does this included piece belong, and what parent does it complete?

collegeVersion.heading: Work packages bridge scope to planning without becoming the schedule
collegeVersion.body:
Decomposition stops at a level useful for managing and planning the work. A lowest-level component is commonly called a work package. A work package is not necessarily one person’s task, one day of effort, or one fixed template field. It is a bounded component that can be described well enough to relate it to the information a project needs, such as its expected result, assumptions, resources, estimate, risks, or later activities. The amount of detail that is useful depends on the project’s size, uncertainty, and need for control. More levels are not automatically more accurate; excessive detail can hide the big picture and become costly to maintain.

A WBS and a schedule have a close relationship, but they answer different questions. The WBS asks, “What included components and results must be accounted for?” A schedule asks, “What activities will occur, in what order, with what dependencies and dates?” From a work package such as “event-direction signs,” a team may later identify activities to draft, review, print, and place signs. Those activities must be sequenced, but their sequence is not the WBS. Starting a WBS as a chronological to-do list can hide a missing deliverable because a list may look busy while omitting a necessary result.

The same distinction limits what a WBS can promise. It can give scope a structure that supports estimates, schedule construction, communication, and risk analysis. It cannot ensure that an estimate is accurate, force a dependency to disappear, settle competing priorities, or guarantee that people will use the final result. A useful WBS is a transparent model of the current scope, not a substitute for stakeholder judgment, a contractual document, or an organization’s governance process. Later lessons treat scheduling, dependencies, estimating, and responsibility-related planning in more detail.

vocabulary.definition: A hierarchical, deliverable-oriented decomposition that organizes the included scope of a project into smaller components.
The act of dividing a broad project result or component into smaller, understandable, and manageable parts.
A verifiable product, result, capability, or component that project work is intended to produce or make available.
A higher-level WBS component that is represented in more detail by one or more child components.
A lower-level WBS component that contributes to explaining the included work of its parent element.
A coverage check that child components together represent all included work of their parent, without extra work outside it.
A lowest-level WBS component defined at a useful level for relating bounded work to later planning information.
A planned action or step that is sequenced over time to help create or deliver a WBS component.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine planning a neighborhood festival. Saying “make the festival happen” is too big to check. A WBS breaks that big idea into parts, such as information for visitors, the event site, and the activities people will use. Each part can break into smaller parts until people can see what belongs. It is like sorting a big collection into labeled boxes before deciding the order in which to pack them.

The 100-percent concept asks whether the small boxes cover everything in their larger box. If the “visitor information” box includes a web page and signs but forgets the required accessibility notice, something is missing. If it includes a permanent advertising campaign for the entire city, it contains extra work that does not belong to this festival project. A WBS makes those questions easier to see before the team turns components into a calendar of actions.
eli10.analogy: A WBS is like a map of the pieces needed to build a large model. The top label names the complete model, and lower labels name its sections and smaller parts. A work package is one small, clear section that can be planned without losing sight of the model it belongs to.
eli10.analogyLimits: A project is not a model kit with every piece supplied and one fixed instruction sheet. New information can justify revising the scope, and real work involves people, uncertainty, and choices. The analogy also does not decide dates, responsibilities, or approval rules.

workedExample: River City Library is hypothetically preparing a one-day neighborhood storytelling festival. Its first WBS level contains four included components: participant experience, event information, site readiness, and project coordination. Under event information, the group identifies a public event page, directional signs, and a participant information sheet. Under site readiness, it identifies venue layout and participant access. The team notices that the access branch has no component for the accessible route from entrance to seating, so the current breakdown fails to cover the stated access parent. It adds an accessible-route plan as a component. Later, the team develops schedule activities such as draft, review, print, and place the directional signs. Those activities come from the WBS component, but they are not themselves the WBS. This is an illustrative planning example, not advice about library operations or approvals.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a chronological task list and calling it a WBS.
commonMistakes.correction: First organize the included result into deliverable-oriented components; later identify and sequence the activities needed for those components.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the 100-percent concept as a promise that nothing will change or go wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: Use it to test coverage of the current defined scope and make later learning or changes visible rather than invisible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using departments or job titles as the main WBS branches.
commonMistakes.correction: Group by project deliverables and component work; use a separate structure if the project needs to show reporting or responsibility relationships.

commonMistakes.mistake: Decomposing until every tiny action is shown regardless of usefulness.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop at a work-package level that supports understandable planning and control for the project’s context.

compareContrast.distinction: A WBS organizes included deliverable components; a schedule sequences activities over time to create or deliver those components.
A deliverable component can occur at any WBS level; a work package is a lowest-level component at a useful planning level.
A WBS groups project scope by results and components; an organizational chart groups people or units by reporting relationship.

keyTakeaway: A WBS is a deliverable-oriented hierarchy for making a project’s included scope visible. The 100-percent concept tests each parent-child branch for complete, bounded coverage, while work packages give later scheduling and planning a manageable starting point.

questionBank.prompt: Which description best defines a work breakdown structure?
options: A hierarchy that decomposes the included project scope into deliverable-oriented components.
A calendar showing the date and duration of every action.
A reporting chart that places project staff under managers.
A list of all risks that might affect a project.
questionBank.explanation: A WBS organizes scope by deliverable-oriented components. A calendar is a schedule, a reporting chart organizes people, and a risk list serves another planning purpose.
questionBank.skill: Recall the defining purpose of a WBS.

questionBank.prompt: What does the 100-percent concept ask a learner to check for a parent WBS element?
options: That the parent will require exactly one hundred hours.
That its child elements cover all included parent work without omitting work or adding work beyond it.
That each child has the same number of activities.
That every project has exactly one hundred work packages.
questionBank.explanation: The concept tests logical coverage and boundaries between a parent and its children; it is not a time estimate, counting rule, or requirement for equal-sized branches.
questionBank.skill: Explain the 100-percent concept.

questionBank.prompt: A festival WBS includes a parent called “event information” with children for a public page and directional signs. The scope also requires a participant information sheet, but the WBS contains no such component. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The WBS is automatically a schedule because it contains two components.
The public page should be assigned to a different department.
The event-information branch may fail the 100-percent concept because an included component is missing.
The team should remove all children and use only one top-level title.
questionBank.explanation: If the information sheet is included scope but has no component, the children do not fully represent their parent. The issue is coverage, not scheduling, staffing, or eliminating decomposition.
questionBank.skill: Apply the 100-percent concept to identify a missing component.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement most accurately explains the relationship between a WBS and a schedule?
options: They are identical because both list project work.
A schedule replaces the WBS once dates are known.
A WBS assigns people, while a schedule defines deliverables.
A WBS identifies included components, while a schedule sequences activities needed to create or deliver them.
questionBank.explanation: The WBS provides a scope-oriented decomposition. A schedule uses time, sequence, and dependencies to plan actions related to those components; neither replaces the other.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish scope decomposition from activity sequencing.

questionBank.prompt: Which item is the best candidate for a work package rather than a broad project goal or a schedule activity?
options: A bounded lowest-level component such as “event-direction signs,” defined well enough for later planning.
Make the festival successful by the end of the year.
Place the finished signs at 9:00 a.m. on event day.
The library outreach department.
questionBank.explanation: A work package is a bounded lowest-level WBS component. The other options are a broad outcome, a timed activity, and an organizational unit.
questionBank.skill: Identify a work package in context.

options: The WBS is automatically a schedule because it contains two components.

title: Scheduling
in30Seconds: A project schedule is a time-based representation of planned work and significant events. It helps people see when activities are expected to occur, how long they are currently expected to take, and when a milestone or review point is expected. A schedule is not a promise that the future will unfold exactly as shown. Estimates rest on assumptions and available information, so a useful schedule makes its current plan visible and can be updated when evidence changes.
whyItMatters: Without a shared time picture, people can agree on a project’s goal and still misunderstand when work, reviews, or needed decisions are expected. Scheduling creates a basis for discussing timing, not a guarantee of a finish date. It also encourages a useful distinction: a task list says what work exists, while a schedule places work and milestones in time. Students who can read that distinction can evaluate a proposed timeline, notice uncertainty in estimates, and avoid treating one early date as a fact about the future.
learningObjectives: Define a project schedule as a time-based representation of planned activities and significant events.
Distinguish an activity, a duration estimate, a milestone, and a schedule baseline.
Explain why a duration estimate depends on assumptions and available information rather than providing certainty.
Apply basic schedule concepts to a short hypothetical timeline without calculating a critical path.
Analyze why comparing actual progress with a baseline is useful but does not automatically determine what decision to make.

collegeVersion.heading: A schedule puts planned work on a time horizon
collegeVersion.body:
A project schedule is a representation of planned work and important events in time. It may be shown as a calendar, timeline, table, board, or another format suited to the work. What makes it a schedule is not the software or visual style; it is the connection between planned activities and time. A simple schedule can show that draft content is expected during one period, a review is expected later, and a public demonstration is expected after that. It gives a group a common object for discussing timing instead of relying on scattered recollections of dates.

A task list and a schedule are related, but they answer different questions. A task list can say that a team must prepare materials, test a sign-up process, and conduct a demonstration. The schedule asks when each item is currently expected to occur and how much time is allowed for it. That distinction matters when someone says, “We have all the tasks.” A complete list may still provide no shared view of timing. Conversely, dates alone can be misleading if no one knows what work or review each date represents.

Scheduling is not restricted to a predictive approach. A project that works in short cycles can schedule the boundaries of a cycle, planned review opportunities, or a target window for a demonstration while leaving some detailed work to be learned later. A hybrid project can use longer-range milestones with shorter-range planning. The educational point is modest: a schedule expresses a current time plan. It should not be presented as a universal method, a certification procedure, or a guarantee of results.

collegeVersion.heading: Estimates and milestones make timing discussable
collegeVersion.body:
An activity is a planned unit of work. A duration estimate is the currently expected amount of working time or elapsed time associated with an activity, depending on how the schedule is defined. The wording matters: an estimate is a reasoned approximation based on the information, assumptions, and conditions known now. It is not a promise that an activity will require exactly that amount of time. A team may learn that a review needs more participants, an assumption about available equipment was wrong, or new information changes the work. Treating an estimate as certain can hide those conditions rather than improve planning.

A milestone is a significant point or event in a schedule. For example, “pilot materials ready for review” may be a milestone. It draws attention to an important state, decision, or observable point without serving as a detailed description of every activity that leads to it. “Finish the flyer” is an activity; “community review completed” can be a milestone. A milestone may have no duration of its own in a schedule, but it can still help people coordinate a conversation, review, or handoff.

Consider a hypothetical neighborhood workshop project. The group expects to draft materials during the first week, seek accessibility feedback in the second week, revise materials in the third week, and hold a pilot session at the end of that week. The pilot is a milestone: it marks a meaningful event. The draft and revision are activities with estimates that rest on assumptions such as reviewer availability. The example does not establish the right duration for another project. It shows how labels make a proposed timeline easier to examine.

collegeVersion.heading: A baseline supports comparison; uncertainty still remains
collegeVersion.body:
A schedule baseline is an approved version of a schedule model used as a reference for comparison. In a classroom case, it might be the agreed timeline a team uses to ask whether the current plan and actual progress differ. Baselines make change visible: if a planned review moves from week two to week three, the group can identify the difference rather than silently replacing the old date. That visibility supports a better conversation about what changed and what is now known. It does not make a baseline a prediction machine or a rule that a plan may never change.

Comparing current progress with a baseline produces information, not an automatic decision. A delay could reflect a changed requirement, an inaccurate estimate, a newly discovered constraint, or a choice to improve a result. The appropriate response depends on context and authority. This lesson therefore does not prescribe who should authorize a change, how resources should be reassigned, or what a real organization must document. It simply distinguishes noticing a variance from deciding how to manage it.

Schedules are most useful when they retain their uncertainty. People can record relevant assumptions, distinguish a target from a commitment when their setting uses those terms, and update the time picture as better evidence appears. Updating is not an admission that planning failed; it can be a response to learning. It also cannot guarantee that all future work will occur as forecast. Detailed dependency networks, critical-path methods, PERT calculations, resource leveling, and formal schedule-control systems are valuable specialized topics, but they are outside this introductory lesson.

vocabulary.definition: A time-based representation of planned project activities, events, and their expected timing.
A planned unit of work that contributes to a project result or a significant event.
A reasoned approximation of how long an activity is expected to take under stated assumptions.
A significant point or event in a schedule that marks an important state, review, or decision.
An approved version of a schedule model used as a reference for comparing planned and actual timing.
A difference observed between a schedule reference and current timing, progress, or forecast.
A condition treated as true for planning purposes even though later evidence may confirm or change it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
A schedule is like a school-play calendar. It does more than list jobs such as learn lines, paint scenery, and test lights. It places those jobs in time: practice this week, scenery review next week, dress rehearsal on Friday. That lets people see what is expected when.

The dates are a plan, not magic. If the paint does not arrive or an actor gets sick, the calendar may need an update. A milestone is a big marker, like dress rehearsal. A duration estimate is a best current guess about how long a job will take. Looking at the old calendar and the new situation helps people notice a change, but it does not tell them by itself what to do.
eli10.analogy: A schedule is like a travel itinerary. Stops represent activities, travel windows represent estimated durations, and a hotel check-in can be a milestone. The itinerary helps travelers coordinate their plan in time.
eli10.analogyLimits: A project is not a trip with all routes and reservations fixed in advance. Work can reveal new information, and project decisions involve people, constraints, and authority that an itinerary cannot resolve. The analogy also does not calculate dependencies or decide who approves a real change.

workedExample: The River City Library hypothetically plans a one-evening digital-skills workshop. Its draft schedule places material preparation in the first week, a volunteer review in the second, revisions in the third, and the pilot workshop at the end of that third week. The pilot workshop is a milestone because it is a significant event; preparing the materials is an activity. The two-week preparation estimate assumes that existing devices are available and that two volunteers can review the materials. When one volunteer is unavailable, the team compares the current situation with its schedule baseline and notices that the review may move. That observation does not dictate a response or promise a new date. It identifies an uncertainty that the people responsible can discuss. The example is illustrative, not operational advice for a library.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a task list as though it automatically provides a schedule.
commonMistakes.correction: Add timing and meaningful events so readers can see when work is currently expected to occur.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a duration estimate as a guaranteed finish time.
commonMistakes.correction: State relevant assumptions and recognize that estimates can change as evidence improves.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a milestone as a substitute for the activities that lead to it.
commonMistakes.correction: Use a milestone to mark a significant point while separately identifying the work needed to reach it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a baseline comparison tells a team exactly what action to take.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the comparison to make a variance visible, then consider its cause and context through the appropriate process.

compareContrast.distinction: A task list identifies work; a schedule connects planned work and significant events to time.
A duration estimate approximates how long an activity may take; a milestone marks a significant event or point in the schedule.
A baseline is a reference version of the plan; a current forecast reflects the latest expected timing based on available information.

keyTakeaway: A schedule makes a project’s current time plan visible through activities, estimates, and milestones. A baseline can reveal differences from that plan, while uncertainty and new evidence mean the schedule remains a tool for discussion rather than a promise.

title: Dependencies
in30Seconds: A dependency is a logical relationship that says how one planned activity relates to another. Finish-to-start means one activity must finish before the next can start; start-to-start and finish-to-finish allow specific kinds of overlap; start-to-finish is a rare reverse relationship. Dependencies can be internal to a project or external, involving something outside its control. Recording the relationship, its reason, assumptions, and constraints makes the current plan easier to question and update; it does not guarantee timing.
whyItMatters: A calendar can show dates without explaining why work is ordered that way. Dependencies expose those reasons: a review may need a draft, two activities may begin together, or a project may need information from outside the team. That visibility helps people distinguish a genuine condition from a habit or an unstated guess. It also prevents a common error: treating an outside approval, delivery, or decision as though the project can command it. Learning to state dependencies precisely improves discussion of a plan without claiming to predict its finish date or calculate a critical path.
learningObjectives: Define a dependency and distinguish predecessor and successor activities.
Explain the basic meanings of finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish, and start-to-finish relationships.
Distinguish internal dependencies from external dependencies.
Identify the role of assumptions and constraints when documenting a dependency.
Apply dependency concepts to a short hypothetical example without calculating a critical path or estimating a schedule.

collegeVersion.heading: Dependencies state a relationship, not merely two dates
collegeVersion.body:
A dependency is a logical relationship between planned activities. It says that an event concerning one activity affects when another activity may start or finish. The activity supplying the condition is the predecessor; the activity affected by it is the successor. These labels describe the relationship, not job rank or importance. A predecessor may be a short review activity, and a successor may be a much larger activity.

The central question is not, “Which date comes first on a calendar?” It is, “What condition connects these activities?” For example, if a team cannot begin a public review until a draft exists, the review has a logical connection to the draft. A schedule may show both on dates, but the dependency explains why placing the review earlier would not make sense. Conversely, two activities that happen to be dated one after another do not automatically have a dependency. They may simply have been placed that way for convenience.

A dependency is also not a claim that a certain date will be met. It gives a model of a relationship using current information. If its underlying condition changes, the relationship or its interpretation may need review. That is why a dependency should be understandable to the people reading the plan: it is evidence for a proposed order of work, not an invisible rule produced by scheduling software.

collegeVersion.heading: Four relationship types describe different conditions
collegeVersion.body:
Finish-to-start (FS) is the familiar sequence: the successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes. “Review the completed draft” after “prepare the draft” is an FS relationship if the review needs the completed version. FS does not mean the review begins immediately after drafting; another condition could still delay it. It names one boundary that must be satisfied.

Start-to-start (SS) means the successor cannot start until the predecessor starts. It can express a limited kind of overlap. For example, a team may begin monitoring sign-up questions only after registration opens. Once registration has started, monitoring may start too, although it need not begin at the exact same moment. Finish-to-finish (FF) means the successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes. A project could require both a participant guide and its accessibility check to be complete before the guide is considered ready; the activities may proceed in parallel, yet the check cannot be treated as complete before the guide it checks is complete.

Start-to-finish (SF) means the successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts. It is the fourth possible combination, but it is unusual and easy to misread because the successor may occur earlier in time than the predecessor. A handover from an existing support shift to a new shift can illustrate the idea: the existing shift cannot end until the replacement shift has begun. In beginner planning, it is often better to state the real handoff condition plainly than to introduce a complicated relationship. No type is a magic shortcut; the useful type is the one that accurately communicates the condition.

collegeVersion.heading: Internal, external, assumptions, constraints, and documentation
collegeVersion.body:
An internal dependency connects activities within the project’s own planned work. “Draft the guide before review” is internal if both activities belong to the same project. An external dependency connects the project to something outside that schedule or project boundary, such as an outside group’s decision, an external system’s availability, or a required piece of information from another effort. The distinction matters because the project may be able to change, split, or clarify internal work, but it may not control the external event. Calling an external dependency “internal” can create a false impression of authority.

Assumptions and constraints add useful context. An assumption is a condition used for planning because it is treated as true for now, such as expecting a partner to provide a data file in a particular format. A constraint is a limit or condition that narrows what can be done, such as a fixed venue-access window or an interface that cannot accept a certain file type. Neither label makes a future event certain. Recording them helps a reader see why the relationship was modeled and what should be checked if the plan changes.

A lightweight dependency record can name the predecessor and successor, relationship type, whether it is internal or external, the reason for the link, its source or point of contact when relevant, and any assumptions, constraints, or review date. The record makes a conversation auditable: a reader can ask whether the condition is real, still current, and owned by the right boundary. It does not tell a real organization who must approve work, force an external party to act, or solve a delay. Critical-path calculations, duration estimates, buffers, and detailed network analysis are separate topics and are intentionally outside this lesson.

vocabulary.definition: A logical relationship in which one planned activity affects when another activity may start or finish.
The activity whose start or finish provides a condition for a related successor activity.
The activity whose start or finish is affected by a stated relationship with a predecessor.
A relationship in which the successor cannot start until the predecessor activity has finished.
A relationship in which the successor cannot start until the predecessor activity has started.
A relationship in which the successor cannot finish until the predecessor activity has finished.
A less common relationship in which the successor cannot finish until the predecessor activity has started.
A relationship tied to activity, information, or an event outside the project’s own schedule or boundary.
A limit or condition that restricts the available ways project work can be planned or performed.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine a school play. Before actors can rehearse with the finished props, the props must be ready. That is a dependency: one thing changes what another thing can do. The prop-making job is the predecessor, and the rehearsal is the successor.

Most dependencies are simple: finish the props, then start the rehearsal. Sometimes jobs can overlap. The person checking costumes might start as soon as costume sewing starts, but cannot finish the final check until sewing is finished. A project can also wait for something outside the team, such as the school confirming that the auditorium is available. That is an external dependency, because the play group does not control the confirmation.
eli10.analogy: Dependencies are like rules for connecting pieces in a domino setup. One piece may need another piece placed first, while two separate lines can be built at the same time. The connections reveal which actions are related.
eli10.analogyLimits: A project is not a row of dominoes that always falls in one fixed way. People can revise work, conditions can change, and an outside group may not act when expected. The analogy also does not choose dates, calculate a critical path, or tell a real organization how to approve a change.

workedExample: River City Library hypothetically plans a one-evening digital-skills workshop. Its project activities include prepare a draft handout, begin an accessibility review, finish the handout, and complete the review. The team records an SS relationship between preparing the draft and beginning the review: the reviewer can start giving early feedback only after draft work has started. It records an FF relationship between finishing the handout and completing the review, because the review cannot be complete until the handout version being reviewed is complete. The workshop also depends on an external confirmation that a community partner will supply a projector. The record labels that link external, identifies the partner confirmation as its source, and notes the assumption that the projector supports the required connection. This documentation clarifies the current plan; it does not guarantee the partner’s action, estimate a date, or decide how the library should respond if the confirmation changes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every pair of consecutive calendar entries a dependency.
commonMistakes.correction: State the actual condition that connects activities; dates alone do not prove a logical relationship.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading finish-to-start as a command that the successor must begin immediately.
commonMistakes.correction: It says the successor cannot start before the predecessor finishes; other conditions can still affect its start.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating an external dependency as work the project team controls.
commonMistakes.correction: Label the external boundary, source, and relevant assumption so the control limit is visible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a relationship label without explaining its rationale or constraint.
commonMistakes.correction: Record why the link exists and what condition should prompt a review.

compareContrast.distinction: FS prevents the successor from starting before the predecessor finishes; SS prevents it from starting before the predecessor starts.
FF prevents the successor from finishing before the predecessor finishes; SF prevents the successor from finishing before the predecessor starts and is less common.
An internal link connects activities within the project plan; an external link depends on an event, information source, or activity outside the project boundary.
An assumption is treated as true for current planning; a constraint is a limiting condition that narrows available choices.

keyTakeaway: Dependencies make the logic behind a plan visible. Choose a relationship type that states the real condition, distinguish internal work from external reliance, and document relevant assumptions and constraints so the relationship can be examined without mistaking it for a guaranteed date.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best defines a finish-to-start relationship?

The successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts.
Both activities must start at exactly the same time.
The predecessor and successor have no scheduling relationship.

questionBank.explanation: Finish-to-finish means the successor, here the review, cannot finish until its predecessor, the guide, has finished. The activities may overlap.

questionBank.prompt: A project cannot run a workshop until a community partner confirms that it will provide a projector. The partner is outside the project team. How should the dependency be classified?

As a start-to-finish relationship because a projector has a start date.
As an external dependency because the needed confirmation comes from outside the project boundary.
As a duration estimate because the confirmation may take time.

questionBank.prompt: Which description best fits a start-to-finish relationship?

title: Critical Path Basics
in30Seconds: In a schedule network, the critical path is the continuous path whose planned duration is longest. Under the schedule's current logic and duration assumptions, it determines the earliest possible project finish. Activities on that path commonly have zero total float, so a delay can move the forecast finish by the same amount unless something else changes. Critical path is a model result, not a promise: changing durations, logic, constraints, or progress can change the result.
whyItMatters: Critical-path thinking directs attention to timing relationships that currently control a project's forecast completion. It helps students avoid two costly misunderstandings: treating every activity as equally urgent and assuming an activity is safe to delay simply because it is not visibly late. The concept also teaches a healthy limit on schedule claims. A calculated critical path depends on the activity network and its assumptions; incomplete links, unrealistic durations, or date constraints can make the displayed path misleading. It is a way to examine a time model, not a guarantee or an instruction to ignore other project concerns.
learningObjectives: Define a critical path as the longest-duration continuous path in a schedule network under current inputs.
Explain why that path determines the earliest modeled completion date.
Distinguish total float from an activity's duration and from a promise of schedule safety.
Identify the critical path in a small, labeled hypothetical network by comparing complete path durations.
Analyze how changed logic, durations, constraints, or progress can change a schedule's critical path.

collegeVersion.heading: The critical path is a result of a schedule network
collegeVersion.body:
A critical path is not simply a list of important tasks or the tasks that feel most difficult. It is a result computed from a schedule network. A network represents activities and the logical relationships that connect them from a project start toward a finish. When the durations on each complete route are considered, the critical path is the continuous route with the longest planned duration. The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) describes it as the path of longest duration through the sequence of activities; it establishes the modeled earliest completion date or minimum duration. The word critical therefore refers to timing in that particular model, not to an activity's prestige, cost, or moral importance.

Why does the longest route control the finish? Work on different routes may proceed in parallel, but the project cannot finish before every required route leading to completion has finished. If one route takes 12 working days and another required route takes 15, the 15-day route is the limiting route in this simplified model. Completing the shorter route in 10 days would not make the overall finish earlier than 15 days. This is a high-level explanation of network logic, not a substitute for building a detailed network. The Dependencies topic owns the relationship types and the Estimating topic owns how duration estimates are developed. Here, the important point is that the critical path is calculated from current connections and current duration assumptions.

A schedule can have more than one critical path when multiple complete routes tie for the longest duration. That possibility matters because attention should not collapse onto a single line merely because a diagram uses one highlight color. Similarly, an activity may be operationally important without lying on the current critical path. A safety review, a scarce specialist, or a stakeholder decision can deserve careful attention for reasons that a duration calculation does not capture. Critical-path analysis is one lens for time-based coordination, not a ranking of everything a project values.

collegeVersion.heading: Float describes modeled timing flexibility
collegeVersion.body:
Total float, also called total slack, is a schedule-model measure of how much an activity can slip before the project forecast finish is affected. GAO notes that activities on the critical path generally have the least total float. In an unconstrained network, critical activities have zero float: a one-day delay in one of those activities moves the forecast finish one day unless the delay is mitigated by some other change. This is the source of the usual classroom shorthand that critical-path work has no timing cushion. The shorthand is useful only when its conditions are remembered.

Float is not extra calendar time that someone may spend casually, and it is not the same thing as an activity's duration. An activity might take three days and have two days of total float, meaning the schedule model currently allows its timing to move by up to two days before the overall forecast finish changes. That does not establish that a delay has no consequences for a handoff, a person, quality, cost, or another local milestone. It also does not mean the activity will remain noncritical. A delay consumes float; once the cushion is gone, the activity may become critical in the updated model.

The critical path and float are only as informative as the network. GAO cautions that missing or incorrect logic, unrealistic durations, unstatused work, and date constraints can distort float and critical-path results. For that reason, a displayed zero-float task should prompt questions about the model as well as attention to the work: Are the relevant activities represented? Are their links plausible? Are the duration assumptions still current? This lesson does not prescribe a process or tool for answering those questions. It establishes the interpretive limit: a computed result is evidence about a schedule model, not proof that the future will unfold that way.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading a small hypothetical network without overclaiming
collegeVersion.body:
Consider a hypothetical student-exhibit project with two required routes after a common start. Route One contains Create labels (3 days), Print labels (2 days), and Install labels (1 day), for 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 days. Route Two contains Prepare display cases (2 days) and Set up display cases (5 days), for 2 + 5 = 7 days. If the listed activities and connections are complete, Route Two is the critical path because seven days is longer than six. The model's earliest finish is seven days after the common start, not six, because the exhibit requires both routes.

The arithmetic is deliberately simple and fully stated. It assumes the listed activities can begin when their shown predecessor is complete, use the same working-day calendar, have no unlisted resource conflict, and contain no imposed date constraint. It also assumes the two routes meet only at the common start and final exhibit readiness. Those assumptions are not details to hide; they are part of why the result is conditional. If printing actually cannot begin until a display-case decision is made, the logic changes. If setting up the display cases changes from five days to three, the longest route may change or both paths may tie. Critical path is recalculated when the model's meaningful inputs change.

This example is not an estimate for an actual exhibit and does not advise anyone how to sequence work, assign people, or recover a delay. It is a transparent arithmetic illustration: compare complete route durations, identify the longest route, and state the assumptions. Larger schedules require careful data, status updates, and context-sensitive judgment. A critical path can focus timing conversations, but it cannot by itself establish a realistic deadline, resolve competing priorities, or guarantee delivery.

vocabulary.definition: A representation of project activities and the logical connections used to model paths from a start toward a finish.
The continuous path with the longest planned duration through a schedule network under its current inputs.
An activity on the current critical path of a schedule model.
The amount an activity can slip in a schedule model before the project forecast finish is affected; it is also called total slack.
The planned amount of working or elapsed time assigned to an activity in a schedule model.
A condition or imposed date that limits when an activity may start or finish in a schedule model.
The modeled connections that express how activities are sequenced or related in a schedule.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine two routes through a museum before opening. One route needs six minutes of work and the other needs seven. Even if the six-minute route finishes early, the museum cannot open until the seven-minute route is done. In a schedule picture, that longer route is the critical path.

A little timing cushion is called float. If a job can move two minutes without changing opening time, it has two minutes of float in the current plan. Jobs on the critical path often have no such cushion. But the picture can change: a job may take longer than expected, a connection may be missing, or the plan may change. The critical path is a helpful calculation about today's plan, not a prediction machine.
eli10.analogy: Think of packing two required bags for a trip. One bag takes six minutes to pack and the other takes seven. You cannot leave until both are ready, so the seven-minute bag sets the earliest departure in that simple plan.
eli10.analogyLimits: Projects do not behave like two independent bags. Activities can have complex connections, calendars, constraints, resource limits, and changing information. The analogy shows why the longest required route controls a simple finish time; it does not calculate a real schedule or decide what work deserves attention.

workedExample: A hypothetical student-exhibit plan has two routes after a shared start. Route One is Create labels for 3 working days, then Print labels for 2 days, then Install labels for 1 day. Its path total is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 working days. Route Two is Prepare display cases for 2 working days, then Set up display cases for 5 days. Its path total is 2 + 5 = 7 working days. Assuming both routes are required, each listed connection is complete, they share the same calendar, and no other constraints or resource conflicts apply, Route Two is the critical path and the modeled earliest finish is 7 working days. Route One has 1 day of path difference in this simple illustration. If Set up display cases slips one day and nothing else changes, the modeled finish becomes 8 days; if its duration instead becomes 3 days, Route One becomes longer at 6 days. The example illustrates conditional arithmetic, not an operational recommendation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling the activity with the longest individual duration the critical path.
commonMistakes.correction: Compare the total duration of complete connected paths; a path is a route, not one activity.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating zero float as proof that a schedule is accurate.
commonMistakes.correction: Zero float is a model result; check whether logic, durations, status, and constraints make the model credible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a noncritical activity can be delayed without any consequence.
commonMistakes.correction: Float concerns the modeled project finish, not every handoff, cost, quality, or stakeholder effect.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the critical path never changes.
commonMistakes.correction: Recalculate after meaningful changes to durations, logic, constraints, or progress; another path can become longest.

compareContrast.distinction: A critical path is a complete connected route with the longest total duration; one long activity alone does not determine it.
Float is modeled timing flexibility before the forecast finish changes; duration is the planned time assigned to the activity itself.
The path is a result of current schedule inputs; it does not guarantee a finish date or remain fixed when inputs change.

keyTakeaway: The critical path is the longest-duration connected route in a schedule network and therefore controls the model's earliest finish. Its activities commonly have the least float, but both path and float are conditional on credible current logic, durations, constraints, and progress.

questionBank.prompt: In a schedule network, what does the critical path identify?
options: The activity with the greatest budget.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes total float?
options: It is the total length of every activity in a project.
It is a promise that a delayed activity has no consequences.
It is the number of staff assigned to a path.
It is the modeled amount an activity can slip before the project forecast finish is affected.
questionBank.explanation: Total float measures modeled timing flexibility relative to the forecast finish. It is neither activity duration nor a guarantee about all consequences of a delay.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish total float from duration and certainty.

questionBank.prompt: A hypothetical network has two complete required routes: Route A totals 4 + 3 = 7 days, and Route B totals 2 + 6 = 8 days. Under the stated network assumptions, which route is critical?

Route A, because it has an activity lasting 4 days.
Both routes, because each contains two activities.
Neither route, because critical paths cannot be calculated from durations.
questionBank.explanation: Compare total durations of complete required routes. Route B totals 8 days, longer than Route A's 7, so it controls the modeled earliest finish in this simple case.

title: Milestones
in30Seconds: A milestone is a significant point or event that makes progress, a review, a decision, or a handoff visible in a project’s current schedule. It is not the same as a task, which is work someone performs, or a deliverable, which is a result produced by work. “Accessibility review complete” can be a milestone; drafting the review materials is a task, and the reviewed materials are a deliverable. A milestone communicates a meaningful state, but it does not prove that every surrounding detail is settled.
whyItMatters: Teams often say a project is “on track” without agreeing on what evidence would support that statement. Well-chosen milestones make important points visible enough to discuss: Was the prototype actually reviewed? Is a decision needed before later work proceeds? Has a result been handed over? This is valuable for shared understanding in predictive, adaptive, and hybrid work. A milestone is not a promise of success, a substitute for a task list, or a universal approval rule. Learning to separate the event from the work and evidence around it helps students read a schedule more critically and communicate uncertainty honestly.
learningObjectives: Define a milestone as a significant project point or event rather than a duration estimate or task.
Distinguish a milestone, a task, a deliverable, and a decision point.
Explain how observable evidence can support a claim that a milestone has been reached.
Analyze whether a proposed milestone communicates a meaningful state to relevant people.
Describe how milestone information can support schedule communication without guaranteeing a result.

collegeVersion.heading: A milestone marks a meaningful state
collegeVersion.body:
A milestone is a significant point or event in a project’s current time plan. It helps a group see and discuss a state that matters: a design has been reviewed, a pilot has occurred, a handoff is ready, or a decision is needed. The label is useful because it concentrates attention on an event without pretending to describe all the work that surrounds it. A schedule can contain many activities, but not every activity needs to be presented as a milestone. Calling every calendar entry a milestone makes the important points harder to find.

Milestones are planning and communication devices, not guarantees. “Pilot session completed” records a significant event; it does not itself establish that every participant learned equally well or that the project will achieve every intended benefit. A planned milestone also differs from an achieved one. A date on a schedule may show when a group currently expects a review to occur. Evidence from the review is needed before people accurately communicate that it happened. This distinction keeps a schedule from being mistaken for a report of reality.

The particular milestones that matter depend on the project and its delivery approach. A predictive plan may make phase reviews prominent. An adaptive effort may use a demonstration or feedback event as a recurring checkpoint. A hybrid effort can combine longer-range decision points with shorter-cycle reviews. None of these labels makes one approach universally better. The general question is whether the named event gives relevant people a clearer view of progress, uncertainty, or a needed conversation.

collegeVersion.heading: Tasks, deliverables, and decision points answer different questions
collegeVersion.body:
A task is a planned unit of effort: interview participants, draft instructions, test a sign-up form, or prepare a review meeting. It describes work to be done. A deliverable is a result created or completed for use, review, or handoff, such as a draft guide, a tested form, or a summary of findings. A milestone marks a meaningful point, which can be associated with tasks and deliverables without being identical to either. “Prepare the pilot guide” is a task; “pilot guide” is a deliverable; “pilot guide ready for review” may be a milestone.

A decision point is a milestone-like event at which a relevant choice needs to be considered or recorded. For example, after a prototype review, people with appropriate responsibility might decide whether the current direction is suitable to continue exploring. The decision point does not tell a real organization who must approve a change or what choice must be made. It makes the need for a decision visible. Confusing it with an automatic authorization can lead a learner to infer authority that a schedule entry does not create.

The distinction also prevents an empty label. “Work continues” is usually too vague to help someone determine what state has been reached. “Prototype feedback collected and summarized” identifies an event with a clearer connection to evidence. Still, a clear milestone need not list every detailed task or impose a specific template. It should be intelligible enough that people can ask what it means, why it matters, and what would show it has occurred.

collegeVersion.heading: Evidence and communication make a milestone useful
collegeVersion.body:
Evidence is information a person can examine when deciding whether a milestone has been reached. The appropriate evidence depends on the milestone. For “community review completed,” it might include the reviewed version, a record that the review occurred, and a summary of feedback. For “pilot delivered,” it might include the completed session and a brief record of what was observed. Evidence is not automatically proof that a project is correct, finished, or successful; it supports a narrower claim about the stated event.

Milestone communication should name the current state and any important uncertainty. Saying “review scheduled for Thursday” is different from saying “review completed Thursday; two questions remain open.” The first reports an expectation, while the second reports an observed event and a remaining condition. This precision lets recipients distinguish a target, an accomplishment, and an unresolved issue. It is particularly important when a milestone is connected to a decision point, because a meeting occurring does not necessarily mean a decision has been made.

Consider a hypothetical city-library project that is preparing a short digital-skills workshop. The team plans tasks to draft a handout, recruit reviewers, and hold a feedback session. The handout is a deliverable. “Accessibility feedback reviewed” is a milestone, supported by the reviewed handout and a feedback summary. If the summary identifies an unresolved keyboard-navigation question, the milestone can still truthfully communicate that the review happened while separately reporting the open question. That is not a schedule calculation or a recommendation about an organization’s approval process; it is careful use of evidence in project communication.

vocabulary.definition: A significant point or event that makes an important project state, review, decision, or handoff visible.
A planned unit of work performed to contribute to a project result or event.
A result produced by project work that can be used, reviewed, accepted, or handed over.
A stated event at which relevant people need to consider or record a choice.
Information that can be examined to support a bounded claim about whether an event or condition occurred.
The transfer or making available of a result, responsibility, or information for another person or group to use.
A concise account of the current project state, including relevant progress, uncertainty, and open matters.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine planning a school science fair. “Build the display board” is a task because it is work. The finished board is a deliverable because it is something made. “Board ready for teacher review” is a milestone: a big marker that tells everyone an important moment has arrived. The milestone needs something to back it up, such as the actual board and a note that the teacher looked at it.

You can also have a milestone called “choose experiment topic.” That is a decision point. It tells people a choice is needed, but it does not decide the choice by itself. If the teacher review happens but asks for changes, you can honestly say the review happened and also say what remains open.
eli10.analogy: A milestone is like the checkpoint stamp on a hiking route. The stamp shows that a traveler reached a named place; packing a bag and walking there are the tasks, and the map or gear can be deliverables. A checkpoint helps people communicate where the traveler is.
eli10.analogyLimits: Project events can need different kinds of evidence, may happen in parallel, and can involve decisions by people with different responsibilities. A checkpoint stamp also cannot predict the rest of the route or decide what a real project team should do next.

workedExample: River City Library hypothetically prepares a digital-skills workshop. The team drafts an accessible handout, asks volunteers to review it, and records feedback. Drafting and requesting feedback are tasks. The handout and feedback summary are deliverables. “Accessibility feedback reviewed” is a milestone because it marks a meaningful event in the work. The team can support that status with the reviewed version, a dated feedback summary, and a short list of unresolved questions. If one question about keyboard use remains open, the update should not say “all accessibility issues resolved.” It can accurately say that the review milestone was reached and that a decision or additional work remains. The example supports schedule communication; it does not set a real library’s policy or approval process.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every task a milestone.
commonMistakes.correction: Use milestones for significant events or states; retain tasks for the work that leads to them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a deliverable as the same thing as the event of reviewing or handing it over.
commonMistakes.correction: Name the result and the significant event separately when both matter.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reporting a planned milestone as completed.
commonMistakes.correction: Distinguish what is scheduled from evidence that the event occurred.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a decision-point label grants authority or settles an issue.
commonMistakes.correction: It signals a choice for the appropriate people to consider; it does not dictate their process or outcome.

compareContrast.distinction: A task describes work to perform; a milestone marks a significant point or event.
A deliverable is a result; a milestone can mark the result becoming ready, reviewed, or handed over.
A planned milestone is an expectation in the current plan; an achieved milestone is supported by evidence that the named event occurred.
A decision point makes a needed choice visible; a decision is the choice actually made by the appropriate people.

keyTakeaway: Milestones make meaningful project states visible. Separate them from tasks and deliverables, support achieved status with suitable evidence, and communicate both progress and unresolved conditions without treating a schedule entry as a guarantee.
