title: Justice
in30Seconds: Justice is a family of concepts about how people should be treated, not a single rule. Distributive justice asks who should get what share of goods, opportunities, and burdens. Retributive justice asks what punishment wrongdoers deserve. Procedural justice concerns the fairness of the process itself, and corrective and restorative justice address repairing wrongs. Several influential theories—egalitarian, Rawlsian, desert-based, utilitarian, and libertarian—offer different answers, and describing them is not the same as endorsing them.
whyItMatters: Disputes about who should receive scarce scholarships, what counts as fair punishment, or whether a process was fair are disputes about justice. These questions appear in civic life, law, policy, and everyday decisions, and people often talk past each other because they mean different things by the word. Knowing how philosophers distinguish distributive, retributive, procedural, and corrective or restorative justice makes disagreement more precise: the parties can see whether they are arguing about an allocation, a punishment, a process, or a remedy. Studying competing theories also builds the habit of describing views fairly before evaluating them—useful in academic work, professional deliberation, and any setting where people must justify how benefits and burdens are shared.
learningObjectives: Define justice as a family of related concepts applied to actions, laws, policies, and social structures.
Distinguish distributive, retributive, procedural, and corrective or restorative justice.
Explain strict egalitarianism, Rawls's justice as fairness and difference principle, Nozick's entitlement theory, utilitarian welfare-based views, and desert-based views.
Identify the difference between describing a theory and endorsing it.
Analyze a hypothetical allocation using several distributive criteria without assuming one theory is correct.
Explain standard tensions such as equality versus desert versus need, and efficiency versus fairness.

collegeVersion.heading: Justice is a family of concepts
collegeVersion.body: Justice is used in ordinary talk as if it were one thing, but philosophical discussion treats it as a family of concepts applied to different targets: individual actions, laws, public policies, and whole social structures. The same word can express several different questions. Distributive justice asks how benefits and burdens—goods, income, opportunities, jobs—should be shared among people. Retributive justice asks what punishment wrongdoers deserve and what makes punishment proportional. Procedural justice asks whether the process by which a decision or allocation is made is fair, independently of how the resulting outcome looks. Corrective justice demands that a wrongful loss be repaired, for example by returning stolen property, and restorative justice names contemporary approaches that emphasize repairing harm to victims, offenders, and communities rather than punishment alone. Keeping these questions separate is the first skill of this topic: an argument that a punishment was unfair and an argument that a distribution was unfair are different arguments.

collegeVersion.heading: Distributive justice: who should get what
collegeVersion.body: Distributive justice is the branch of the family that asks who should get what. It concerns the frameworks—laws, institutions, policies—whose effects distribute benefits and burdens across a society, and it also applies to smaller decisions such as how a club divides a limited fund. Distributive principles vary along several dimensions: what is being distributed (income, wealth, opportunities, jobs, welfare), who the recipients are, and on what basis the distribution should be made. A classic example survives from Aristotle: if there are fewer flutes than people who want them, he suggested giving them to the best players—distribution according to excellence, a desert-like criterion. Modern discussions typically contrast criteria such as equality, desert, and need, and no criterion is self-evidently the right one for every good. The question “who should get what, and why?” is the question distributive theories answer differently.

collegeVersion.heading: Five influential distributive theories
collegeVersion.body: Philosophers have proposed many distributive principles, and five families dominate current discussion. Strict egalitarianism holds that every person should receive the same level of material goods and services, commonly justified by the moral equality of persons. John Rawls's justice as fairness allows inequalities only under strict conditions: in particular, his difference principle permits social and economic inequalities only when they make the least advantaged members of society materially better off than they would be under strict equality. Desert-based views hold that people should get what they deserve through their actions; contemporary proposals typically ground desert in contribution, effort, or compensation, following the Lockean idea that people deserve the fruits of their own labor. Welfare-based principles, of which utilitarianism is the most famous variant, treat material goods as valuable only insofar as they increase welfare, so distributions are assessed by their effects on overall well-being. Robert Nozick's entitlement theory takes a different route: a distribution is just if everyone is entitled to their holdings through just acquisition and just transfer, so justice tracks the history of holdings rather than any overall pattern. These five families disagree about the unit of distribution and the justification for it, and each has influential defenders and critics.

collegeVersion.heading: Describing theories, weighing tensions
collegeVersion.body: Presenting these theories side by side is not the same as choosing among them. A survey can state what a view claims, the reasons its defenders offer, and the objections its critics raise, while leaving judgment to the reader. The same discipline applies to the standard tensions the theories expose. Equality, desert, and need pull in different directions: an equal share ignores differences in contribution, a desert-based share can ignore differences in need, and a need-based share can ignore effort. Efficiency can also conflict with fairness: strictly equal bundles of goods can be inefficient because voluntary trades could make some people better off without harming anyone else, yet the resulting inequality may still trouble a defender of equality. Recognizing these tensions does not dissolve them. It clarifies what the disagreement is about, which is usually the first step toward a defensible judgment. No theory in this lesson is presented as the obvious winner.

vocabulary.definition: A family of concepts concerning how people, actions, laws, policies, and institutions should treat individuals fairly.
The part of justice concerned with how benefits and burdens, such as goods, income, and opportunities, should be allocated among people.
The part of justice concerned with what punishment wrongdoers deserve, typically punishment proportional to the seriousness of the wrong.
The fairness of the process by which an allocation or decision is made, considered apart from the fairness of the resulting outcome.
The remedial demand that a wrongdoer restore or compensate a victim for a wrongful loss, such as returning stolen property.
An approach to wrongdoing that focuses on repairing harm to victims, offenders, and communities, for example through restitution or reconciliation.
The distributive principle that every person should receive the same level of material goods and services.
Rawls's rule that social and economic inequalities are permitted only if they make the least advantaged members of society better off than under strict equality.
Nozick's view that a distribution is just when everyone holds what they acquired through just acquisition and just transfer.
What a person merits on the basis of their actions, such as effort, contribution, or the costs they bear.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: When people say something is unjust, they usually mean one of a few different things. They might mean good things were shared out wrongly, or that someone was punished more than they deserved, or that the rules of the game were rigged, or that a wrong was never fixed. Philosophers call these distributive, retributive, procedural, and corrective or restorative justice. The word “justice” covers all of them. Different theories answer the sharing question differently: equally, according to need, according to desert, to maximize overall well-being, or according to how things were acquired. No theory wins by default; each has arguments and limits.
eli10.analogy: Think of a family sharing a weekend cabin. Distributive justice is the question of who sleeps in which room. Procedural justice is whether the family agreed on a fair way to decide—say, a draw or oldest-chooses. Retributive justice is what happens when someone breaks the rules. And corrective or restorative justice is how the family makes things right again, like repairing a window someone broke.
eli10.analogyLimits: Families often settle these questions by habit, mood, or affection, and everyone can still feel treated fairly enough. Theories of justice, by contrast, demand explicit reasons and can pull in different directions: a fair procedure can produce an outcome that feels unequal, and repairing a harm does not settle who should have had the room in the first place.

workedExample: A neighborhood association receives a one-time grant and must decide how to use it. A strict egalitarian proposes splitting the money equally among all households. A member who favors desert argues that the volunteers who maintain the community garden contributed most and deserve a larger share. A utilitarian-minded member suggests spending everything on repairs that benefit everyone, because that raises overall well-being. A Nozick-style view asks instead whether the money was fairly acquired in the first place, so that its later use can follow voluntary decisions. The group is not choosing between “just” and “unjust” answers so much as between competing criteria of justice—and naming which criterion each proposal uses is the first step toward a reasoned decision.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating justice as only a matter of courts and punishment.
commonMistakes.correction: Justice also includes how goods, opportunities, and burdens are distributed; the courtroom is just one of its settings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming one theory, such as egalitarianism, is the obviously correct view.
commonMistakes.correction: The major theories are influential positions with arguments and limits; this lesson describes them without picking a winner.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing procedural fairness with outcome fairness.
commonMistakes.correction: A fair procedure can still produce an outcome some members consider unequal; procedural and substantive justice are separate questions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Equating retributive justice with vengeance or harshness.
commonMistakes.correction: Retributive justice is about proportionate punishment and rules out punishing the innocent; it is distinct from vengeance.

compareContrast.distinction: Asks how benefits and burdens should be shared among many people versus demands that a wrongdoer repair a wrongful loss to a particular victim.
Concerns the fairness of the process by which a decision is made versus the justice of the final allocation itself.
Focuses on giving wrongdoers the proportionate punishment they deserve versus repairing harm to victims, offenders, and the community.

keyTakeaway: Justice is a family of concepts—distributive, retributive, procedural, and corrective or restorative—and the major theories offer competing criteria for applying them. Describing those views fairly is different from endorsing one.

questionBank.prompt: Which kind of justice asks how benefits and burdens such as goods, income, and opportunities should be allocated among the members of a society?
options: Distributive justice
Retributive justice
Corrective justice
Procedural justice
questionBank.explanation: Distributive justice concerns the allocation of benefits and burdens among people. Retributive justice concerns proportionate punishment, corrective justice concerns repairing wrongful losses, and procedural justice concerns the fairness of the process.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the definition of distributive justice

questionBank.prompt: According to Rawls's difference principle, when are social and economic inequalities permitted?
options: Only when every person receives exactly the same material goods and services
Whenever they result from voluntary exchanges between consenting adults
Only if the inequalities make the least advantaged members of society materially better off than they would be under strict equality
Whenever they maximize the total happiness of the society as a whole
questionBank.explanation: The difference principle permits inequalities only when they benefit the least advantaged. Strict equality is egalitarian, voluntary exchange is closer to Nozick's approach, and maximizing total happiness describes a utilitarian standard.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the content of the difference principle

questionBank.prompt: A garden committee has extra seeds, and one member argues that the people who planted and watered the garden all season deserve a larger share of the harvest. Which approach to distributive justice does this argument most closely resemble?
options: Strict egalitarianism
A desert-based principle
Rawls's difference principle
Nozick's entitlement theory
questionBank.explanation: Rewarding people according to their work contribution is the mark of a desert-based principle. Strict egalitarianism would divide equally, the difference principle targets the least advantaged, and the entitlement theory looks to how holdings were acquired and transferred.
questionBank.skill: Matching an argument to a distributive theory

questionBank.prompt: A club awards one workshop seat by random draw, and members agree the outcome is fair even though nobody had an independent claim to the seat. Which description best fits this case?
options: Perfect procedural justice, because the procedure guarantees the substantively just outcome
Substantive justice, because the winner deserved the seat
Corrective justice, because the draw repaired a prior loss
Pure procedural justice, because there is no independent standard for the outcome beyond the procedure itself
questionBank.explanation: When no independent standard for the outcome exists, fairness rests entirely on the procedure, which is Rawls's pure procedural justice. Perfect procedural justice guarantees a just result, and substantive and corrective justice address different questions.
questionBank.skill: Applying the procedural justice distinction to a case

questionBank.prompt: Why does describing a theory of justice fairly matter even for someone who does not endorse it?
options: Because a theory can be described accurately only by someone who accepts it
Because presenting competing views without selecting a winner lets readers evaluate the arguments for themselves
Because accurate description automatically counts as endorsement
Because endorsement is required before a theory's claims can be stated
questionBank.explanation: A survey can state a view's content and the reasons behind it while leaving judgment to the reader; description and endorsement are different acts. The other options wrongly tie description to acceptance.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing description from endorsement in philosophical writing

title: Rights
in30Seconds: A right is an entitlement or claim that generates duties in others: if you have a right that your neighbor not enter your yard, your neighbor has a corresponding duty. Rights may be moral, grounded in moral reasons, or legal, recognized by law, and a right can be one without the other. Negative rights demand non-interference; positive rights demand provision. Wesley Hohfeld distinguished claims, privileges, powers, and immunities. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is the best-known attempt to name universal rights, though its foundations remain debated.
whyItMatters: Rights language shapes law, politics, medicine, and everyday disputes. When a patient questions a treatment, a renter challenges an eviction, or a community contests a development, each side typically claims a right. Understanding what a right is, and what kind of right is being claimed, clarifies what would settle the dispute: a change in law, a new duty, or a clash of genuine entitlements. The same distinctions used in courtrooms appear in moral arguments about privacy, speech, and aid. Studying rights equips students to analyze such claims precisely rather than merely repeat them.
learningObjectives: Define a right as a claim or entitlement that generates duties in others.
Distinguish moral rights from legal rights and explain why a right can be one without the other.
Distinguish negative rights from positive rights and explain why the boundary between them is debated.
Identify Hohfeld's four basic incidents - claims, privileges, powers, and immunities - and their correlatives.
Explain the correlativity thesis that a claim-right of one person corresponds to a duty of another.
Present the debates over universality, group rights, and conflicting rights neutrally.

collegeVersion.heading: What a right is: claims and entitlements
collegeVersion.body: In philosophy, a right is standardly analyzed as an entitlement or claim that generates duties in others. If you have a right that your landlord give notice before entering, the landlord has a corresponding duty toward you. Rights talk is not merely a way of describing what people want; it asserts that someone is owed something - an action, a forbearance, or a recognized status. That is why rights language is powerful in disputes: it shifts the question from "What would be nice?" to "What is owed?"

collegeVersion.heading: Moral rights and legal rights
collegeVersion.body: A central distinction separates moral rights from legal rights. A legal right is one recognized and protected by the law of a particular jurisdiction: its existence can be checked by locating the relevant statute, regulation, or court decision. A moral right is grounded in moral reasons rather than in any legal code. Because the two are independent, a right can be one without the other. A right may be morally justified yet unprotected by law, and a law may grant a right that many people think morally unjustified. The two kinds interact: moral arguments often aim at changing the law, and legal recognition can make a moral right enforceable.

collegeVersion.heading: Negative rights and positive rights
collegeVersion.body: Rights are also often sorted by what they require of others. A negative right entitles its holder to non-interference: the right against assault, for example, requires others to refrain from attacking. A positive right entitles its holder to provision of some good or service: a right to welfare assistance requires others to supply it. The distinction is popular among normative theorists, especially those with a libertarian leaning, but it is not uncontroversial. Critics note that enforcing any right costs resources, and that many rights mix elements of both, so the boundary between negative and positive rights is debated rather than fixed.

collegeVersion.heading: Hohfeld's map of rights
collegeVersion.body: Early in the twentieth century, the American legal theorist Wesley Hohfeld argued that "a right" is not one thing but several, and he distinguished four basic incidents. A claim-right correlates with a duty owed to the right-holder: the employee's claim to wages pairs with the employer's duty to pay. A privilege (or liberty) is simply the absence of a duty not to do something: you have a privilege to pick up a shell on the beach because you have no duty not to. A power is the ability to alter one's own or another's rights or duties: making a promise creates a claim in the promisee. An immunity is protection against another's power: a witness's right against self-incrimination blocks others from changing that position. Most real-world rights are molecular combinations of these incidents.

collegeVersion.heading: Human rights and their contested foundations
collegeVersion.body: Human rights are rights held simply because one is human. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948, is the best-known statement of the idea; its Article 1 declares that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Drafted after the Second World War by a UN commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, the Declaration sets out thirty articles and has been translated into more than 500 languages. Its philosophical foundations, however, remain contested. Some justify human rights by features of human status, in a deontological spirit; others justify them by their good consequences, in an instrumental spirit; and moral relativists deny that any moral truths hold universally.

collegeVersion.heading: Rights and duties: correlativity
collegeVersion.body: On the correlativity thesis, rights and duties come in pairs: if A has a right against B, then B has a duty to A. Hohfeld's table makes the logic explicit: every claim-right correlates with a duty in at least one duty-bearer. Correlativity does not say that duties exhaust rights, or that rights are nothing but duties looked at from the other side. It says that a claim-right without any corresponding duty would be incomplete, because the point of the claim is that someone owes something.

collegeVersion.heading: Three live debates
collegeVersion.body: Three debates recur in the philosophy of rights, and this lesson presents them without deciding them. Are rights universal? Universalists hold that all persons have the same basic rights; relativists treat rights as products of particular societies and histories. Do groups have rights? Some theories, such as the interest theory, can extend right-holding to groups and institutions, while other accounts insist rights belong to individuals. Can rights conflict? Rights often appear to conflict - a public right to protest against a government's duty to keep order, for example - and philosophers differ over whether such conflicts are real or merely apparent, and over which right should prevail.

vocabulary.definition: An entitlement or claim that others owe something: an action, a forbearance, or a recognized status.
A right grounded in moral reasons, whether or not the law recognizes it.
A right recognized and protected by the law of a particular jurisdiction, whether or not morality endorses it.
A right to non-interference, such as a right against assault.
A right to provision of some good or service, such as a right to welfare assistance.
In Hohfeld's scheme, a right that correlates with a duty owed to the right-holder.
In Hohfeld's scheme, the absence of a duty not to do something.
In Hohfeld's scheme, the ability to alter one's own or another's rights or duties.
In Hohfeld's scheme, protection against another's power to alter one's rights or duties.
The thesis that every claim-right of one person corresponds to a duty of another person.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Rights are a way of saying who owes what to whom. When you say "I have a right to," you are usually saying that other people, or institutions, are not allowed to do certain things to you, or must provide certain things for you. That is why rights come with duties attached: your right not to be pushed around is your neighbor's duty not to push. Some rights are written into law, like the ones in a lease; others are moral claims that exist even when no law protects them. People disagree about which rights everyone has, whether groups can have rights, and what happens when two rights pull in opposite directions. Knowing the vocabulary helps you say which kind of right you mean.
eli10.analogy: Think of a right as a ticket that other people are required to honor. If you hold a seat ticket at a theater, the staff owe you a seat and other patrons have a duty not to take it. A legal right is a ticket the theater printed and enforces. A moral right is a ticket that binds people even when no one printed it - like the promise you owe a friend because you gave your word.
eli10.analogyLimits: Tickets are issued by someone and can be revoked, while moral rights are usually thought to attach to persons rather than to be granted by anyone. Tickets also rarely conflict, whereas rights frequently appear to - two valid tickets to the same seat is a better image for a rights conflict, and philosophers disagree about how to resolve those.

workedExample: Priya lends her bicycle to her neighbor Sam for the weekend, and they agree Sam will return it by Sunday evening. In Hohfeld's terms, Priya now holds a claim-right that Sam return the bicycle, and Sam holds the correlative duty to Priya. Sam also holds a privilege: he has no duty not to ride the bicycle this weekend. Priya retains a power, because she can waive her claim and let Sam keep the bicycle longer, which would change Sam's duty. If Sam damaged the bicycle, Priya's rights against him would be different claims, and her rights against everyone else - that strangers not take the bicycle - are separate claim-rights with their own duty-bearers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every right is a legal right.
commonMistakes.correction: Moral rights exist independently of law, and law can also create rights that many people consider morally unjustified; a right can be one without the other.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading "negative" and "positive" rights as "bad" and "good" rights.
commonMistakes.correction: The terms describe what the right requires: non-interference (negative) versus provision of a good or service (positive).

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing a privilege with a claim-right.
commonMistakes.correction: A privilege is the absence of a duty not to act; a claim-right correlates with a duty owed to you by someone else.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming that if rights appear to conflict, at least one of them is not a genuine right.
commonMistakes.correction: Rights often appear to conflict, and philosophers disagree about whether such conflicts are real or merely apparent; the appearance of conflict does not by itself show that either claim is bogus.

compareContrast.distinction: Grounded in moral reasons versus recognized and protected by law; each can exist without the other.
Entitlement to non-interference versus entitlement to provision of a good or service; the boundary is debated.
A right that correlates with another's duty versus the mere absence of a duty not to act.

keyTakeaway: Rights are claims that generate duties in others. Distinguishing moral from legal, negative from positive, and Hohfeld's four incidents makes rights talk precise enough to analyze real disputes without pretending the hard debates are settled.

questionBank.prompt: In Hohfeld's analysis, which right is best described as an entitlement that correlates with a duty owed to the right-holder?
options: A privilege (or liberty) - the absence of a duty not to act.
A claim-right - the correlate of a duty owed to the right-holder.
A power - the ability to alter rights or duties.
An immunity - protection against another's power.
questionBank.explanation: A claim-right is defined by its correlative: if A has a claim that B do φ, then B has a duty to A to do φ. A privilege is the absence of a duty not to act, a power is the ability to alter rights or duties, and an immunity protects against another's power, so none of the others matches.
questionBank.skill: Identify the Hohfeldian claim-right and its correlative duty.

questionBank.prompt: Which term best describes a right that entitles its holder to non-interference, such as a right against assault?
options: A positive right, which requires others to provide a good or service.
An inalienable right, which cannot be given up.
A customary right, which exists by local convention.
A negative right, which requires others to refrain from interfering.
questionBank.explanation: A negative right entitles its holder to non-interference, and the right against assault is the classic example. Positive rights entitle the holder to provision of a good or service, while inalienability and customary origin are separate features of rights.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish negative from positive rights by what they require.

questionBank.prompt: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris in which year?
questionBank.explanation: The UDHR was proclaimed on 10 December 1948 as General Assembly resolution 217 A. The year 1945 is when the United Nations was founded, while 1954 and 1966 are dates associated with later human-rights instruments, the European Convention on Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
questionBank.skill: Recognize a landmark date in the history of human rights.

questionBank.prompt: Jordan promises to water a friend's plants while the friend is away. On the correlativity thesis, what follows?
options: The friend holds a claim-right against Jordan, and Jordan holds a duty to the friend.
Jordan holds a claim-right against the friend, and the friend holds a duty to Jordan.
Both hold privileges, so neither has any duty.
The friend holds an immunity, so Jordan cannot change the arrangement.
questionBank.explanation: The promise creates a claim in the friend and a correlative duty in Jordan to water the plants - that is exactly what correlativity says. The other options reverse the parties, confuse privileges with claims, or misapply the idea of immunity.
questionBank.skill: Apply the correlativity of claim-rights and duties to a promise.

questionBank.prompt: Two neighbors dispute a loud outdoor gathering: one claims a right to host it, and the other claims a right to quiet enjoyment of home. What does this case best illustrate?
options: That one of the rights is always stronger, regardless of circumstances.
That at least one of the neighbors has no genuine right.
That rights can appear to conflict, and philosophers disagree about whether the conflict is real or merely apparent.
That rights cannot conflict because every right is absolute.
questionBank.explanation: Rights often appear to conflict - the public's right to protest against a government's right to keep order is a standard example. Philosophers disagree about whether such conflicts are genuine or only apparent (as specificationists argue) and about which right should prevail. The case does not show that one right is always stronger, that either claim is bogus, or that rights never conflict.
questionBank.skill: Analyze an apparent conflict of rights without adjudicating it.

title: Equality
in30Seconds: Equality is a contested ideal. People agree it matters but disagree about what it requires: equal treatment under the rules, equal opportunities, or equal outcomes. Philosophers distinguish formal equality from substantive equality, and formal from fair equality of opportunity. They also ask what should be equalized, whether resources, welfare, or capabilities, as Amartya Sen urged. Egalitarian, sufficiency, and priority views offer rival answers, and the leveling-down objection challenges equality of outcome. Even whether equal treatment means identical treatment remains disputed.
whyItMatters: Equality claims shape scholarship decisions, hiring, access to buildings and programs, and public policy. When people say a rule is unfair because it is unequal, they usually have one of these conceptions in mind, and different conceptions support different conclusions. Learning to separate formal equality, equality of opportunity, and equality of outcome, and to see why the question of what should be equalized matters, turns a rhetorical slogan into a precise disagreement. The same tools carry into later study of justice, rights, and applied ethics, and into evaluating any policy that distributes opportunities or resources.
learningObjectives: Define equality as a contested concept in social and political philosophy.
Distinguish formal equality from substantive equality.
Distinguish formal equality of opportunity, fair equality of opportunity, and equality of outcome.
Explain the capabilities approach to the question of what should be equalized and attribute it to Amartya Sen.
Contrast egalitarian, sufficiency, and priority views, and explain the leveling-down objection to equality of outcome.
Analyze whether equal treatment requires identical treatment, using feminist and disability critiques.

collegeVersion.heading: Equality is a contested concept
collegeVersion.body: In ordinary talk, equality sounds straightforward: treat everyone the same. In philosophy, it is among the most contested ideals of social and political thought. As Ronald Dworkin observed, people who praise or disparage equality disagree about what they are praising or disparaging. Equality is not identity: equality names a correspondence between different persons with respect to some feature, while identity means being one and the same thing. A claim that two students are equal is incomplete until it says equal in what respect: before the law, in resources, or in opportunity. Much of the philosophical work on equality is making that respect explicit.

collegeVersion.heading: Formal and substantive equality
collegeVersion.body: The formal principle of equality, often traced to Aristotle, says to treat like cases as like. Students alike in the respects that matter for a grade should receive the same treatment; those who differ in those respects may not. Philosophers disagree about its grounds. Some treat it as a rule of rationality: it is inconsistent to treat equal cases unequally without sufficient reason. Others treat it as a moral principle requiring that unequal treatment be justifiable to those affected. Either way, the formal principle does not answer the hard question of which respects are relevant. Substantive equality goes further. Instead of asking only whether rules are applied consistently, it asks whether people end up with genuinely equal conditions, opportunities, or results. A rule applied identically to everyone can still leave some people unable to participate, and substantive views treat that as an equality problem.

collegeVersion.heading: Equality of opportunity and equality of outcome
collegeVersion.body: Equality of opportunity is a family of views. Formal equality of opportunity requires that positions be open to all, with no legal or coercive barriers, and that selection run as open, merit-based competition. It forbids allocating positions by gender, ethnicity, or similar traits but does not ask why some applicants were better prepared. Fair equality of opportunity, formulated by John Rawls, adds a requirement: people with the same talent and ability and the same willingness to use them should have the same prospects of success regardless of social class of origin. If children in one neighborhood receive far weaker schooling, fair opportunity fails even though applications are open to everyone. Substantive equality of opportunity goes further, addressing both the procedures of competition and the preparation of candidates. Equality of outcome is the more demanding rival: it assesses equality by the results people actually reach. Most egalitarians do not advocate equality of outcome; they defend some form of equality of opportunity, partly because they take individual responsibility seriously.

collegeVersion.heading: Equality of what? Resources, welfare, capabilities
collegeVersion.body: Whatever equality is sought, there remains the question of its metric. Equality of welfare aims at equal well-being but faces the expensive-tastes problem: people with costly preferences would consume a disproportionate share of resources. Equality of resources, associated with Ronald Dworkin, aims at equal holdings of income, wealth, and other resources, but the same resources do different work in different lives. Amartya Sen pioneered the capabilities approach to address this gap. Sen argues that what matters is not the resources people hold but their real freedoms to achieve functionings, the doings and beings that make up a life. In his 'Equality of What?' example, two people with identical resources are not equal if one must spend much of them on a wheelchair just to get around. Because people convert resources into functionings at different rates, equal resources do not guarantee equal capabilities. Martha Nussbaum and others have since developed it in their own directions.

collegeVersion.heading: Egalitarianism, sufficiency, and priority
collegeVersion.body: Theories of distribution also differ over which value should guide us. Egalitarianism holds that equality itself has significant value: other things equal, a more equal distribution is better. The sufficiency view, associated with Harry Frankfurt, holds that what matters is not that everyone has the same but that each has enough; once everyone has enough, remaining differences matter less. The priority view, associated with Derek Parfit, holds that benefiting people matters more the worse off they are, even apart from any comparison. Prioritarians and egalitarians may favor similar policies but disagree about why: priority cares about absolute position, while equality cares about relation to others. The views face different objections, and the choice between them remains a live dispute.

collegeVersion.heading: The leveling-down objection, and equality and difference
collegeVersion.body: One influential objection targets equality of outcome directly. Parfit asks us to imagine a policy that makes everyone equal by making the better-off worse off, without benefiting anyone; intuitively, this seems objectionable, since nobody is helped and somebody is harmed. The objection suggests that what really moves people is not equality but priority, giving extra weight to the worse off. Egalitarians reply that equality can be intrinsically valuable, so a more equal distribution is better in one respect even when it helps no one; some add that for positional goods, such as a vote, leveling down may be appropriate. A separate debate asks whether equal treatment requires identical treatment. Feminist critics of purely procedural equality observe that 'like cases alike' leaves open which respects are relevant. Difference feminists such as Martha Minow argue that equality can require attending to physical, historical, and social differences, and describe dilemmas of difference: taking a difference into account can seem required for equality yet appear to single people out. Disability-focused critiques make a similar point: a rule requiring everyone to climb the same stairs treats everyone identically while excluding a wheelchair user; identical resources can fail people whose conversion of resources into functionings differs. These are contested positions, presented as the debate, not a settled verdict.

vocabulary.definition: The principle that people who are alike in normatively relevant respects should be treated alike, often traced to Aristotle's 'treat like cases as like.'
An approach holding that equality requires attention to actual conditions and outcomes, not only to consistent application of rules.
The ideal that positions and advantages should be open to all, ranging from formal open competition to fair opportunity that equalizes background conditions.
John Rawls's requirement that people with the same talent and willingness to use it have the same prospects of success regardless of social class of origin.
An approach that assesses equality by the results people actually reach, such as income, welfare, or capabilities, rather than by access to competition.
Amartya Sen's framework for evaluating well-being by people's real freedoms to achieve doings and beings, rather than by the resources they hold.
A family of views holding that equality has significant value and that distributions should be evaluated by how equal they are.
The position, associated with Harry Frankfurt, that what matters morally is that each person has enough, not that all have the same.
The position, associated with Derek Parfit, that benefiting people matters more the worse off those people are, even apart from equality.
The objection that a policy which reduces inequality by making the better-off worse off without benefiting anyone is morally objectionable.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Equality sounds simple: treat everyone the same. But philosophers quickly notice that 'the same' is slippery. The same rule can hurt people who are differently situated, and the same resources can do different amounts of work in different lives. So equality debates are really about which comparisons matter: rules, opportunities, outcomes, or what people can actually do and be. Different answers lead to different policies, and reasonable people disagree about which answer is right. The goal of this lesson is not to settle that disagreement but to make it precise.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a school giving every student the exact same pair of shoes, in the same size. That is equal treatment in one sense: everyone gets the same thing. But it is not equal in the sense that matters to the students, because the shoes fit some, pinch others, and fit almost no one well.
eli10.analogyLimits: Shoes are a simple good with an obvious fit test, so the right response seems clear: match the shoe to the foot. In real equality debates there is no obvious test. People disagree about which differences are relevant, about how much responsibility we bear for our choices, and about whether equality or something else, like sufficiency, is the value that should guide us.

workedExample: A community theater sells tickets to a play. Everyone pays the same price and follows the same rules, so formal equality is satisfied. But the theater's only entrance has a flight of stairs, so a patron who uses a wheelchair cannot get in. The ticket policy treats everyone alike, yet it does not give everyone the same real opportunity to attend. Now imagine two applicants for the theater's internship: both may apply, but only one could afford a university theater course that the selection panel rewards. Formal equality of opportunity holds, because the application is open and selection is merit-based. Fair equality of opportunity arguably does not, because social background shaped the applicants' prospects. Which inequalities the theater should address, and with which metric in view, is exactly what the competing conceptions dispute.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming equality means identical treatment in every respect.
commonMistakes.correction: Formal equality requires treating like cases alike in relevant respects; it does not require sameness where people are relevantly different.

commonMistakes.mistake: Conflating equality of opportunity with equality of outcome.
commonMistakes.correction: Equality of opportunity concerns access and fair prospects in competition; equality of outcome concerns the results people actually reach. Most egalitarians defend forms of the former.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating formal equality as automatically sufficient for substantive equality.
commonMistakes.correction: A rule applied consistently can still exclude people who are differently situated; substantive views ask about background conditions and actual results.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the leveling-down objection refutes every egalitarian view.
commonMistakes.correction: The objection is a serious challenge, but egalitarians reply that equality can be intrinsically valuable or grounded in other values; the lesson presents the debate rather than a verdict.

compareContrast.distinction: Formal equality requires consistent treatment of like cases under the rules; substantive equality looks beyond rules to conditions, opportunities, and results.
Formal opportunity requires open, merit-based competition; fair opportunity (Rawls) also requires that social class not shape the prospects of people with equal talent and effort.
Sufficiency (Frankfurt) cares that each person has enough; priority (Parfit) cares that benefits matter more the worse off people are.

keyTakeaway: Equality is a contested ideal, not a single formula. Careful thinking separates formal from substantive equality, opportunity from outcome, and asks which metric, whether resources, welfare, or capabilities, should be equalized.

questionBank.prompt: The formal principle of equality, often traced to Aristotle, is usually stated as which of the following?
options: Treat everyone identically in every respect, regardless of circumstances.
Treat like cases alike, and different cases differently in the relevant respects.
Ensure that everyone ends up with the same amount of resources.
Give priority to whoever is worst off, regardless of how they got there.
questionBank.explanation: Formal equality requires that people who are alike in normatively relevant respects be treated alike. It does not require identical treatment in every respect or equal outcomes, and giving priority to the worst off is the priority view, a different position.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the formal equality principle and its limits

questionBank.prompt: A city announces that a training program is open to all residents and selects participants by a written test. In practice, only applicants who could afford private test-preparation courses pass. Which statement best describes this situation?
options: Formal equality of opportunity is satisfied, but fair or substantive equality of opportunity may not be.
The program achieves equality of outcome because everyone may take the test.
The program violates formal equality of opportunity because entry is not legally restricted.
The program has nothing to do with equality because it uses a test.
questionBank.explanation: Formal equality of opportunity requires only that positions be open to all and selected by merit. Fair equality of opportunity (Rawls) additionally requires that social class not shape prospects for success, so unequal access to preparation can undermine it while formal opportunity remains intact.
questionBank.skill: Applying the distinction between formal and fair equality of opportunity

questionBank.prompt: Two students receive identical scholarships. One student has a disability and must spend a large share of the money on equipment just to get around. Which claim best captures Amartya Sen's point in his 'Equality of What?' argument?
options: The students are equal because their resources are identical.
The students' welfare is equal because both received the same amount.
Equal resources can still yield unequal capabilities, because people differ in converting resources into doings and beings.
The scholarship should be withdrawn because it cannot make the students equal.
questionBank.explanation: Sen argues that evaluating equality requires looking beyond resources to what people can actually do and be, since conversion of resources into functionings varies with personal and social circumstances. Identical resources therefore do not guarantee equal capabilities.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the capabilities approach as a response to the equality-of-what question

questionBank.prompt: The leveling-down objection targets policies that would do which of the following?
options: Make the worst-off better off at some cost to the better-off.
Equalize opportunities by improving schooling for everyone.
Reduce inequality while also improving everyone's position.
Reduce inequality by making the better-off worse off without benefiting anyone.
questionBank.explanation: The objection, associated with Parfit, targets reductions in inequality achieved by worsening the position of the better-off while helping no one. Critics argue this shows priority rather than equality is the underlying value; egalitarians respond that equality can still be valuable in itself.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the leveling-down objection to equality of outcome

questionBank.prompt: A community center requires all members to reach the pool by stairs. The rule applies to everyone, but a member who uses a wheelchair cannot enter at all. Which of the following best captures the philosophical critique of this arrangement?
options: The rule is fair because it treats every member identically.
Equal treatment may not require identical treatment: rules that ignore relevant differences can exclude people who are differently situated.
The center should close the pool rather than change the entrance.
The rule violates the priority view because the member using a wheelchair is not the worst off.
questionBank.explanation: Difference-focused feminists such as Minow and capability theorists argue that purely formal equality can perpetuate disadvantage when it ignores relevant differences. Identical treatment is not automatically equal treatment, because people differ in how resources and rules convert into real opportunities.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing whether equal treatment requires identical treatment

title: Applied Ethics
in30Seconds: Applied ethics is the branch of ethics that examines moral questions as they arise in concrete practices and cases: in medicine, business, technology, the environment, and the professions. It draws on normative theories such as utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics as resources, while particular cases can in turn test and refine those theories. Careful applied analysis states the moral question, checks the relevant facts, names the moral considerations, weighs them, and considers alternatives.
whyItMatters: Moral questions rarely arrive in the abstract; they arrive embedded in real practices, institutions, and constraints. Applied ethics gives students a disciplined way to analyze such questions without reducing them to personal opinion or expecting a single theory to produce an automatic answer. It matters academically because it connects normative theory to concrete cases, practically because professionals, policymakers, and citizens face these questions regularly, and educationally because it builds the habit of checking facts, stating reasons, and revising conclusions honestly when new information appears.
learningObjectives: Define applied ethics as the branch of ethics that examines moral questions in concrete practices and cases.
Distinguish applied ethics from normative ethics and metaethics, and explain how theories and cases inform each other.
Explain reflective equilibrium as a method of adjusting considered judgments and general principles until they cohere, attributing it to John Rawls.
Apply a structured analysis (state the moral question, gather facts, identify considerations, weigh them, consider alternatives) to an ordinary case.
Identify the main domains of applied ethics: bioethics, business ethics, environmental ethics, technology ethics, and professional ethics.
Analyze the limits of applied ethics, including persistent disagreement, the role of facts, and the difference between domain expertise and moral authority.

collegeVersion.heading: From general theory to particular cases
collegeVersion.body: Applied ethics is the branch of ethics that takes up moral questions as they arise within particular practices, institutions, and cases. Where normative ethics asks what general standards should guide conduct, applied ethics asks whether specific actions and practices are morally permissible: whether a particular policy is fair, whether a particular practice is justified, whether a particular decision is right. The distinction is a matter of focus rather than a wall. A question about which principle should govern all policies is normative; a question about this policy, with these facts and these people affected, is applied. Metaethics, the third branch, asks a different kind of question about the meaning and status of moral claims themselves. Applied ethics usually proceeds on the assumption that questions of right and wrong are worth asking, and it examines them where they actually occur.

collegeVersion.heading: Theories as resources, cases as tests
collegeVersion.body: Normative theories supply resources for applied analysis. Consequentialist theories evaluate actions by their outcomes, deontological theories by duties and rights, and virtue-based theories by character and the ideals of a good life; applied ethics consults these approaches across nearly all of its domains. Using a theory is not mechanical. Philosophers debate whether applied questions are settled by deducing an answer from a theory or whether practical reasoning works differently, and many applied arguments draw on several theories at once. The traffic also runs the other way: cases test theories. A carefully constructed case can function as a counterexample to a general view, as the familiar transplant problem does for simple consequentialism. Reflective equilibrium makes this two-way traffic explicit. John Rawls proposed the method in A Theory of Justice (1971): the reasoner treats considered judgments — judgments made under conditions suitable for careful moral deliberation — and candidate general principles as materials to be brought into agreement, revising judgments in light of strong principles and principles in light of firm judgments. Applied and normative ethics thus inform each other rather than running in one direction only.

collegeVersion.heading: A method for analyzing a case
collegeVersion.body: A practical method for a case proceeds through five stages. First, state the moral question precisely: what action, policy, or practice is being evaluated, and by whom. Second, gather the relevant facts. Applied ethics requires considerable empirical knowledge of the practice in question; a conclusion built on a mistaken fact collapses. Third, name the moral considerations — the rights, duties, consequences, values, and commitments that could reasonably bear on the case. Fourth, weigh them honestly, including conflicting considerations rather than hiding them. Fifth, consider alternatives: rarely are only two options available, and institutional or practical alternatives often change the analysis. Facts do not by themselves generate an "ought" conclusion; a moral claim needs a stated reason that connects the facts to a standard. This method makes the reasoning visible and testable. It does not guarantee agreement, but it turns an exchange of conclusions into an exchange of reasons.

collegeVersion.heading: Domains of applied ethics
collegeVersion.body: Applied ethics is organized largely by practice. Bioethics examines moral questions in medicine, health care, and biological research. Business ethics examines commerce, corporate conduct, and the responsibilities of firms to stakeholders. Environmental ethics examines obligations regarding the natural world, non-human animals, and future generations. Technology ethics — including computer and information ethics — examines privacy, algorithmic decisions, and the design and use of digital systems. Professional ethics examines the duties and standards of professions such as law, medicine, and engineering, including the use of codes of conduct. Each domain has its own literature and its own specialists; an expert in one may have little to say in another. Several of these domains are treated in depth in their own lessons.

collegeVersion.heading: Limits: disagreement, facts, and authority
collegeVersion.body: Applied ethics does not promise unanimous answers. Disagreement persists among careful reasoners, and it can stem from different facts, different principles, or different weights assigned to genuine considerations; locating the source of disagreement is itself part of the analysis. Facts matter: empirical knowledge of a practice is part of what makes applied analysis serious. Domain expertise matters too, but it is not moral authority. A physician knows medicine, an engineer knows structures, and a business leader knows markets; none of that knowledge by itself settles the moral question, which requires reasons that others can examine. Finally, this lesson is general education, not individualized advice. Real high-stakes decisions involve specialized evidence, institutional context, and perspectives absent from a classroom scenario, and responsible analysis in such settings identifies what further information and expertise are needed.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of ethics that examines the moral permissibility of specific actions and practices within particular domains.
The branch of ethics that develops and evaluates general principles or standards for moral conduct.
The branch of ethics that investigates the meaning, nature, and status of moral claims and values.
A method in which a reasoner adjusts considered moral judgments and general principles back and forth until they agree; associated with John Rawls.
A moral judgment made under conditions suitable for careful moral deliberation, treated as a starting point for reflective equilibrium.
A feature of a case offered as relevant to its moral evaluation, such as a right, duty, consequence, or value.
The domain of applied ethics concerned with moral questions in medicine, health care, and biological research.
The domain of applied ethics concerned with moral questions in commerce and corporate conduct.
The domain of applied ethics concerned with moral questions about the natural environment and non-human life.
The domain of applied ethics concerned with the moral duties and standards of professions such as law, medicine, and engineering.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Applied ethics is what happens when ethics meets a real situation: a hospital, a company, a new app, a polluted river. It does not start from scratch. It borrows ideas from the big moral theories — consequences, duties, character — and asks which ones help with this particular problem. And the situation talks back: if a rule leads somewhere clearly wrong, the rule may need to change. Applied ethics is a two-way street between principles and cases, with the goal of reaching a judgment that holds together after checking facts, hearing the people affected, and weighing the reasons.
eli10.analogy: Think of applied ethics as test-driving a car. The theories are like the car's features: steering, brakes, engine. You do not choose one feature and ignore the rest; you use what fits the road. The case is the road itself. A sharp turn can reveal that the steering needs adjustment, just as a hard case can reveal that a principle needs refinement. The test drive ends when the car handles the route — when principles and judgments move together smoothly.
eli10.analogyLimits: A car comes with a manual that gives one correct setting for every condition, and a test drive has a definite end. Moral cases do not. People can disagree about which feature matters most, the facts can stay uncertain, and there may be no setting that satisfies everyone. The analogy captures the back-and-forth between theory and case, but not a guarantee of a single right answer.

workedExample: A campus food pantry run by students is offered a steady supply of day-old bread by a grocery chain — on the condition that the pantry stops posting its occasional public statements criticizing the chain's labor practices. The moral question is whether accepting the bread under that condition is right. The facts matter: how much food the pantry currently has, whether other donors exist, what the statements actually said, and who depends on the pantry. The considerations include feeding people in need, keeping the arrangement honest, and whether staying silent would mislead anyone about the chain's practices. The students weigh these, then consider alternatives: asking for the food without the condition, finding other donors, or accepting and issuing a separate, clearly labeled statement. The group may not reach one obvious answer, but the question, facts, considerations, and options are now visible for discussion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating applied ethics as choosing one favorite theory and mechanically deducing the answer.
commonMistakes.correction: Theories are resources, not vending machines; cases can push back against a principle, and careful analysis often draws on more than one theory.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping the facts.
commonMistakes.correction: Applied analysis requires reliable empirical knowledge of the practice; a moral conclusion resting on a wrong fact is unsupported.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing domain expertise with moral authority.
commonMistakes.correction: Knowing a practice deeply informs the analysis, but the moral question is settled by reasons others can examine, not by a practitioner's standing alone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting applied ethics to eliminate disagreement.
commonMistakes.correction: Disagreement can persist over facts, principles, or how considerations are weighed; the value of the method is clearer and more honest reasoning, not guaranteed consensus.

compareContrast.distinction: Examines whether specific actions and practices are morally permissible versus develops and evaluates general principles of conduct.
Asks what should be done in a concrete practice versus asks about the meaning, nature, and status of moral claims.

compareContrast.a: Deductive application of theory to a case
compareContrast.distinction: Moves one way, from principle to verdict, versus moves both ways, adjusting judgments and principles until they agree.

keyTakeaway: Applied ethics examines moral questions in concrete practices, drawing on normative theories while letting cases test them; its disciplined method — question, facts, considerations, alternatives — makes disagreement clearer without promising automatic answers.

questionBank.prompt: Which example below is a question of applied ethics?
options: Whether a specific university housing policy is fair to the students it affects.
What the word 'fair' means and whether moral claims can be true or false.
Which general principle should govern all university housing policies.
Whether students happen to prefer one housing policy over another.

questionBank.prompt: A team analyzing a company's plan to move production overseas gathers wage and safety data, then compares utilitarian, rights-based, and virtue-based readings of the case. What are they doing?

Legal analysis, because they are checking whether the plan is lawful.
Applied ethics that uses normative theories as resources and checks relevant facts.
Showing that normative theories are irrelevant to practical questions.
questionBank.explanation: Gathering empirical facts and consulting several normative theories is the core of applied analysis; A describes metaethics, B describes legal review rather than moral analysis, and D denies the use of theories the scenario actually illustrates.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing how facts and normative theories work together in applied analysis

questionBank.prompt: The method of reflective equilibrium — adjusting considered moral judgments and general principles until they agree — is most closely associated with which thinker?
