title: Healthcare Ethics
in30Seconds: Biomedical ethics asks what is right, fair, and caring in medicine and healthcare. A widely used starting point is the four-principles framework developed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress: respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. These principles identify the moral considerations at stake; they do not automatically settle hard cases. This lesson examines that framework, informed consent, end-of-life questions, and the fair allocation of healthcare resources, and it marks the line between ethical analysis and clinical or legal advice.
whyItMatters: Healthcare decisions touch everyone: what treatments to accept, who decides when a person cannot decide, and how scarce care is shared. These questions combine facts, values, and conflicting loyalties, which is why they never reduce to a single formula. Studying biomedical ethics gives you a vocabulary and a method for analyzing such questions, whether in a philosophy course, a health-related career, or public debate, without pretending that one framework ends the disagreement. It also trains the habit of separating reasoned ethical analysis from clinical judgment and legal advice.
learningObjectives: Define biomedical ethics and identify the range of questions it examines.
Explain the four-principles framework of Beauchamp and Childress and why it is a framework rather than a formula.
Describe what informed consent requires and why it functions as an ethical and legal norm.
Distinguish the contested positions on killing versus allowing to die and on advance directives.
Analyze a hypothetical healthcare case by identifying the relevant principles, the affected parties, and the remaining disagreements.

collegeVersion.heading: Biomedical ethics studies moral questions raised by medicine and healthcare
collegeVersion.body:
Biomedical ethics — the ethics of healthcare practice and policy — examines moral questions that arise in medicine, healthcare, and the life sciences. The term bioethics was coined in 1970 by the American biochemist Van Rensselaer Potter to name the study of ethical issues that emerge with advances in biology, technology, and medicine. Its questions range widely: how much say a patient has in their own treatment, who gets access to care and on what basis, whether human experimentation is ever acceptable, and how life-and-death decisions should be made. In a philosophy course, biomedical ethics is a branch of applied ethics: it brings general moral concepts to a specific domain of practice rather than inventing a separate morality for medicine.

The most widely used starting point is the four-principles framework developed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in their influential book Principles of Biomedical Ethics. It organizes the field around respect for autonomy (honoring a person's informed, voluntary choices about their care), beneficence (acting for the patient's good), non-maleficence (avoiding harm), and justice (fairness in the distribution of benefits and burdens). The principles are prima facie and mid-level: each identifies a genuine moral consideration, none automatically overrides the others, and hard cases require specification and balancing. The framework is a map of the moral terrain, not a formula that computes a single answer.

collegeVersion.heading: Informed consent: a norm with three elements
collegeVersion.body:
Informed consent is the requirement that a medical intervention or research participation be authorized by the person who will undergo it. The standard idea is that consent should be informed, voluntary, and given by someone with decision-making capacity: a person receives adequate information, understands what has been disclosed, and agrees freely rather than under coercion. Three elements recur across accounts: information, comprehension, and voluntariness. Consent so understood is a legitimacy requirement — without it, substantial intrusions into a person's body are ethically impermissible, even when caregivers mean well and others would benefit. When a person lacks the capacity to decide, similar rules operate through other channels, such as a previously expressed advance directive or a proxy decision-maker.

Informed consent is also a legal norm, reflected in human-rights documents and in law; legal details vary by jurisdiction and context, and this lesson describes the norm generally rather than as legal advice. Two clarifications matter for a philosophy course. First, informed consent is not paperwork: a signature is evidence of a process, not proof that the process succeeded. Second, consent requirements can conflict with beneficence — a patient's informed refusal may frustrate caregivers who believe treatment would help — which is why the framework asks for open weighing rather than automatic deference in either direction.

collegeVersion.heading: End-of-life ethics: killing, allowing to die, and advance directives
collegeVersion.body:
End-of-life ethics examines how life-sustaining treatment may be forgone and who decides. A central distinction is between killing a patient and allowing a patient to die: allowing to die typically means withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment, such as a ventilator or resuscitation, so that death occurs from the underlying condition. Many people and legal systems treat the distinction as morally significant — a physician who stops treatment at a patient's request is not doing the same thing, in this view, as a physician who administers a lethal substance. But the distinction is contested. Philosophers such as James Rachels have argued that in paradigm cases the intent and the outcome are the same, so the difference between acting and omitting cannot bear the moral weight alone. This lesson presents the dispute as open, not settled.

Advance directives are one response to the question of who decides when a person can no longer decide. A living will records wishes for future care; a directive may instead name a surrogate decision-maker. The ethical literature distinguishes a substituted-judgment standard (reconstruct what the patient would have wanted) from a best-interests standard (decide what is good for the patient now). Whether an earlier directive should bind a later, changed self is philosophically contested — questions of personal identity and of autonomy across time are genuinely disputed — so advance directives are best described as helpful but context-dependent tools, not automatic answers.

collegeVersion.heading: Justice in healthcare and the limits of ethical analysis
collegeVersion.body:
Justice in healthcare concerns fairness in who receives care and how the benefits and burdens of healthcare systems are distributed. Some hold that healthcare has a special moral importance, while others treat it more like an ordinary commodity; for philosophy, even defining equal access already requires value judgments about what should count. When resources are scarce, choices about allocation are unavoidable. Rationing questions — whether to favor the worst off or those most likely to benefit, whether modest benefits for many outweigh significant benefits for few — produce reasonable disagreement among people who share the same general values. Philosophers have proposed fair-process approaches, such as accountability for reasonableness, in which allocation and coverage decisions are made through procedures that seek mutually justifiable reasons, publicity, and revisability. This lesson presents these positions neutrally and endorses none.

Finally, ethical analysis has limits. It clarifies concepts, identifies the values at stake, and tests arguments; it is not clinical judgment, institutional policy, or legal counsel. This lesson is general education: it uses ordinary hypothetical cases to practice analysis, and it does not offer individualized medical or legal advice for anyone's particular situation.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of ethics that examines moral questions arising in medicine, healthcare, and the life sciences.
The approach in biomedical ethics, developed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress, built on respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice as prima facie principles.
A person's capacity to make decisions about their own life and care; respecting autonomy means honoring informed, voluntary choices.
The principle of acting for the good of others, for example by promoting a patient's welfare.
The principle of avoiding harm, captured by the traditional medical injunction to do no harm.
In healthcare, fairness in the distribution of benefits and burdens, including access to care and the allocation of scarce resources.
Voluntary agreement to a medical intervention or research participation, given by a capacitated person on the basis of adequate information and understanding.
A document or instruction recording a person's wishes for future medical care, such as a living will or the designation of a surrogate decision-maker.
The allocation of scarce healthcare resources among competing needs, which raises questions of distributive justice.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Healthcare ethics is careful thinking about the right thing to do in medicine. It asks questions like: Should a person always be told everything about their treatment? Who decides when someone is too ill to decide? If there is only one ventilator, who gets it? Philosophers work on these questions by naming the values at stake — a patient's choices, the goal of helping, the duty not to harm, and fairness — and by checking how those values pull in different directions. The goal is not to compute one perfect answer, but to make the reasoning visible and honest.
eli10.analogy: Think of the four principles as the four legs of a table. A table stands only when all its legs are in place: a healthcare decision usually involves the patient's choice, the aim of helping, avoiding harm, and fairness to others. If you ignore one leg, the whole discussion wobbles. The table holds the case up while you look at it from every side.
eli10.analogyLimits: Where the analogy breaks down: a table's legs have fixed lengths, but ethical principles carry different weights in different cases, and people can disagree about how much weight each one deserves. The framework shows you what to consider, not how much each consideration counts.

workedExample: A community clinic has one remaining appointment slot today. Two patients need it: an older patient with a chronic condition who needs a routine check-up, and a younger patient with new symptoms that could indicate a serious problem. An ethical analysis first identifies the principles at stake: beneficence (helping the patient in greater need), justice (treating patients fairly rather than by who arrived first), and autonomy (both patients choose whether to come in). The analysis does not automatically say who gets the slot; it shows that the decision turns on facts about severity, alternatives, and the clinic's stated policy. Reasonable staff could weigh the case differently, and a fair process for making the decision matters as much as the choice itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the four principles as an algorithm that computes one correct answer.
commonMistakes.correction: The framework identifies moral considerations to weigh; cases still require judgment about facts, conflicts, and how much weight each principle deserves.

commonMistakes.mistake: Presenting the killing-versus-allowing-to-die distinction as a settled rule.
commonMistakes.correction: Withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment is often distinguished from actively ending a life, but the moral significance of that distinction is contested, so it should be presented as a live dispute.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming informed consent is just a signed form.
commonMistakes.correction: Consent is valid only when a capacitated person agrees voluntarily on the basis of adequate information and understanding; paperwork alone does not establish it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the lesson as personal medical or legal advice.
commonMistakes.correction: This is general education about ethical concepts; it is not clinical judgment, institutional policy, or legal counsel for a particular person's situation.

compareContrast.b: A single ethical theory applied mechanically
compareContrast.distinction: The framework offers several prima facie considerations to weigh in context; a single-theory approach claims one master standard decides every case.

compareContrast.b: Allowing a patient to die by withholding or withdrawing treatment
compareContrast.distinction: Some hold the distinction morally decisive; others argue intent and outcome are the same in paradigm cases, so it is a genuinely contested distinction.
Ethical analysis clarifies concepts, values, and arguments in general terms; clinical and legal advice applies specialized knowledge to a particular person's case.

keyTakeaway: Biomedical ethics supplies frameworks — the four principles, informed consent, and the end-of-life and allocation debates — for making healthcare's hardest questions discussable, while leaving genuine disagreement visible rather than erased.

questionBank.prompt: Which four principles form the framework of biomedical ethics developed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress?
options: Respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice
Equality, charity, diligence, and obedience
Honesty, loyalty, mercy, and prudence
Autonomy, efficiency, empathy, and fairness
questionBank.explanation: Beauchamp and Childress's framework names respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice as the four principles; each other option substitutes at least one value (such as efficiency or charity) that is not part of the framework.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the four-principles framework and its originators

questionBank.prompt: Informed consent, as an ethical and legal norm, is generally understood to require what of a patient or research participant?
options: A signed form witnessed by hospital staff
Agreement given voluntarily, with decision-making capacity, on the basis of adequate information and understanding
Approval from the treating physician before any procedure
A written record of the risks discussed with family members
questionBank.explanation: The standard account requires informed, voluntary, decisionally-capacitated consent: adequate information, comprehension, and freedom from coercion. A signature, physician approval, or family consultation can be part of a process but does not by itself constitute valid consent.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the standard elements of informed consent

questionBank.prompt: A patient with decision-making capacity declines a life-sustaining treatment that her physicians believe would help her. Which statement best reflects how an ethical analysis should treat the case?
options: The physicians should proceed, since their medical judgment is authoritative.
The patient's refusal ends the discussion, because no other principle ever applies.
Respect for autonomy supports honoring the refusal, but the analysis should also consider beneficence and the patient's understanding, and weigh the conflict openly.
The case should be decided by whichever principle the hospital usually applies first.
questionBank.explanation: Respect for autonomy generally supports honoring an informed, voluntary refusal, but beneficence and the patient's understanding are also relevant, and the framework calls for weighing the conflict openly rather than deferring to authority or to a fixed rule.
questionBank.skill: Applying the four-principles framework to a refusal-of-treatment case

questionBank.prompt: A hospital has one ventilator and two patients who need it. Ethicists disagree about whether to give it to the patient with the worse condition or to the patient more likely to recover. What does this disagreement show?
options: That the four-principles framework is useless for allocation questions.
That rationing questions are settled by medical facts alone.
That one of the two positions is clearly unethical.
That allocation under scarcity raises genuine conflicts among values such as helping the worst off and producing the greatest benefit, which reasonable people weigh differently.
questionBank.explanation: The disagreement reflects a genuine conflict among values — giving priority to the worst off versus producing the greatest benefit — which reasonable people weigh differently; allocation under scarcity is a contested justice question, not a purely factual or merely procedural one.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a scarcity scenario as a contested justice question

questionBank.prompt: In end-of-life ethics, why is the distinction between killing a patient and allowing a patient to die described as contested?
options: Because no philosopher has ever discussed the difference.

Some hold that withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment is morally different from actively ending a life, while others argue the intent and outcome in paradigm cases are the same, so the distinction cannot do the moral work alone.
Because the law forbids discussing end-of-life questions.
Because allowing a patient to die always causes more suffering than any alternative.
questionBank.explanation: The distinction is contested because some philosophers and legal traditions treat withholding or withdrawing treatment as morally different from actively ending a life, while Rachels-style arguments hold that intent and outcome in paradigm cases are the same, so the distinction alone cannot settle the ethics.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why the killing-versus-allowing-to-die distinction is a live philosophical dispute

title: Technology Ethics
in30Seconds: Technology ethics asks moral questions that arise as technologies are designed, developed, and used. A central idea, associated with thinkers such as Langdon Winner and with design-ethics scholarship, is that technologies are not value-neutral: design choices embody values like privacy, safety, fairness, and access. The field also examines unintended consequences, including the Collingridge dilemma, privacy and consent in data-collecting systems, bias in automated decisions, and who bears responsibility when technology causes harm.
whyItMatters: Every technology carries choices someone made: what data to collect, whom a system helps or burdens, what happens when it fails. Technology ethics makes those choices visible and gives us language to evaluate them. It matters academically because it connects ethical theory to engineering, policy, and daily life; practically because designers, operators, and regulators are making these decisions now; and educationally because questions about surveillance, algorithmic fairness, and accountability are public controversies students will keep meeting. Studying technology ethics does not produce an automatic answer for every case, but it turns vague unease into questions that can be argued about with evidence and reasons.
learningObjectives: Define technology ethics as the domain of applied ethics concerned with the design, development, and use of technologies.
Explain the claim that technologies are not value-neutral, attributing it to design-ethics scholarship such as Langdon Winner's 'artifacts have politics'.
State the Collingridge dilemma and explain why it makes governing new technologies difficult.
Describe documented concerns about privacy, consent, and surveillance raised by data-collecting technologies.
Distinguish statistical, human, and systemic sources of bias in automated decision-making as categorized in NIST research.
Analyze how responsibility for harm caused by an automated system can be distributed across designers, operators, and deployers.

collegeVersion.heading: A domain of applied ethics
collegeVersion.body: Technology ethics brings philosophical analysis to the moral questions that technologies raise in their design, development, use, and governance. Like bioethics or business ethics, it is a domain of applied ethics: it brings general moral considerations — consequences, rights, fairness, responsibility — to a particular kind of human practice. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy characterizes computer and information ethics as an applied ethics that studies the social and ethical impacts of information and communication technology, comparable to established fields such as medical ethics and business ethics. An ordinary question illustrates the domain: should a messaging app collect location data? It is a moral question, but answering it requires understanding how the technology actually works.

collegeVersion.heading: Technologies are not value-neutral
collegeVersion.body: A central idea in the field is that technologies are not value-neutral: design choices embody values. Langdon Winner argued that "artifacts have politics" (1980): some technologies embody specific forms of power and authority, or are strongly compatible with certain social and political relations, and technologies may become political through the value system and structure of power reflected in how they were designed and deployed. Value-sensitive design aims to integrate values of ethical importance into engineering design systematically. These claims are contested: the value-neutrality thesis — that neither technology as such nor individual technologies incorporate values — has defenders, and the SEP presents the dispute as open. The point is not that every design decision is secretly political, but that neutrality cannot simply be assumed: a design can make privacy, safety, fairness, or access easier or harder to protect.

collegeVersion.heading: Unintended consequences and the Collingridge dilemma
collegeVersion.body: New technologies produce consequences no one predicted, which makes governing them awkward. David Collingridge (1980) captured the problem in what is now called the Collingridge dilemma: early in a technology's development, society has more control over outcomes but less capacity to predict them; later, knowledge grows, but control shrinks because the technology is more strongly embedded in society and investors and developers have vested interests. Control is hard early because we do not know what to control, and expensive late because changing an entrenched system costs more. Collingridge proposed making innovation more corrigible and reversible, and making developers and policymakers more accountable for technological choices. Design ethics has its own limit here: critics note that the ethical ramifications of a technology depend not only on its design but on its use, operation, maintenance, and retirement, so no design phase can guarantee an ethical outcome.

collegeVersion.heading: Privacy, consent, and surveillance
collegeVersion.body: Data-collecting technologies raise recurring concerns about privacy. The SEP's survey of privacy and information technology observes that such technologies can reduce individuals' control over their personal data and open the possibility of negative consequences. Consent is the standard protection, but it is imperfect: consent requests interfere with task flows, and users may simply click them away. Surveillance is a further documented concern, and the literature includes the term "surveillance capitalism" for business models built on monitoring and predicting behavior. Power asymmetries run through all of this: those who collect data hold power over data subjects.

collegeVersion.heading: Automated decisions and bias
collegeVersion.body: Automated systems increasingly make or inform decisions about loans, housing, hiring, and benefits. Researchers at NIST distinguish three sources of bias in such systems: statistical bias, prevalent in large-scale datasets; human bias, which enters through data selection, curation, and annotation; and systemic bias, also called institutional or historical bias, rooted in institutional norms, practices, and history. Documented concerns about fairness are especially prominent in consumer finance, housing, and employment. Two points matter for ethics. First, bias need not be deliberate: a system can inherit skew from the data it was trained on or from the practices it was built to reproduce. Second, "the data" is not neutral either — someone chose which data to collect, which variables to keep, and which outcomes to optimize. The detailed ethics of artificial intelligence is its own topic; here the point is that automated decisions deserve scrutiny wherever they are deployed.

collegeVersion.heading: Responsibility and accountability
collegeVersion.body: When an automated system harms someone, who is responsible? A common difficulty is the problem of many hands, a term coined by Dennis Thompson (1980): in collective settings where knowledge and control are distributed across many actors, assigning individual responsibility is hard. The designer chose the model, the operator chose the data, the deployer chose the deployment, and no one person did everything. Philosophers also discuss a "responsibility gap" (Matthias 2004): for systems that learn and adapt, it may be difficult or impossible to hold any human blameworthy, though some philosophers argue responsibility is better understood as distributed across human-technology collaborations. One practical answer is professional: computing professionals apply codes of ethics and standards of good practice. Technology ethics does not settle who must pay in every case; it insists that the question be asked of every actor with a hand in the system.

collegeVersion.heading: The limits of technology ethics
collegeVersion.body: Technology ethics clarifies questions without promising final answers, and the surrounding law is not keeping pace. NIST reports that there is currently no uniformly applied approach among regulators and courts to measuring impermissible bias, and the SEP describes declining clarity and agreement on privacy as creating problems for law, policy, and ethics. Regulations lag because technologies move faster than legislation, and different jurisdictions answer the same question differently. The practical lesson is that ethical analysis and institutional design belong at every stage — early, when change is still cheap, and late, when the stakes are visible — and that honest disagreement about values is part of the subject, not a failure of it.

vocabulary.definition: Philosophical inquiry into moral questions that arise from the design, development, use, and governance of technologies.
The contested view that neither technology as such nor individual technologies or artifacts incorporate values.
Approaches such as value-sensitive design that aim to integrate values of ethical importance into engineering design in a systematic way.
The problem that early in a technology's development society has more control but less knowledge of consequences, while later knowledge grows but control shrinks as the technology becomes entrenched.
Agreement to data processing given after being informed; treated in the privacy literature as an imperfect protection because consent requests are often clicked away.
Systematic skew in the outputs of automated decision systems; researchers distinguish statistical, human, and systemic sources.
Bias rooted in institutional norms, practices, and history rather than in a dataset alone; also called institutional or historical bias.
The difficulty of assigning individual responsibility in collective settings where knowledge and control are distributed across many actors.
Situations in which it may be difficult or impossible to hold humans blameworthy for the actions of automated learning systems (Matthias 2004).

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A smartphone is not just a piece of glass and metal. Every feature was chosen by someone: the app that asks for your location, the feed that decides what you see first, the software that scores a rental application. Technology ethics is the habit of asking who made those choices, what values they built in, and who gets helped or hurt. It starts from the idea that tools are not morally blank. A camera on every street corner is not neutral: it changes who feels watched and who feels safe. The tricky part is timing. When a technology is new, we can still shape it, but we do not yet know what will go wrong. Once it is everywhere, we know the problems, but changing it is expensive and hard. That is why ethics has to sit inside design and policy from the beginning, not arrive after the damage.
eli10.analogy: Think of a new technology as a river. Early on, near the source, the water is shallow and a few sandbags can redirect it cheaply. Farther downstream it is wide, deep, and lined with houses, factories, and farms; changing its course then means moving a town. The Collingridge dilemma is the ethics version of that: easy to shape before you understand it, hard to reshape after you do.
eli10.analogyLimits: A river has no preferences, while technologies are designed by people with values, and people can deliberate and be held accountable. The river analogy also suggests one correct channel, but societies can legitimately disagree about which consequences matter most and how to weigh them.

workedExample: A landlord starts using an automated service that scores rental applications from historical rental and payment data. The system rejects an applicant who actually qualifies; the applicant suspects the score is wrong. The technology-ethics questions line up quickly. What values are built into the scoring design — speed and convenience, or fairness and access? Where could bias enter: the historical data (statistical), the choice of variables (human), or the industry's past practices (systemic)? And if the applicant is harmed, who answers for it — the landlord who deployed the service, the developer who built it, or the company that supplied the data? The Collingridge dilemma adds a governance question: the service is already in use across many properties, so changing it now is costlier than shaping it before launch. None of these questions has an automatic answer, but each is now on the table.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming technology is neutral and only the people using it are good or bad.
commonMistakes.correction: Design choices embody values: Winner's 'artifacts have politics' and value-sensitive design treat the artifact itself as ethically significant, and the value-neutrality thesis is contested, not settled.

commonMistakes.mistake: Waiting until a technology causes problems and then fixing it.
commonMistakes.correction: The Collingridge dilemma says later control is harder and costlier because the technology is entrenched and interests are invested; reflection belongs early as well as late.

commonMistakes.mistake: Blaming 'the computer' or a single person when an automated system harms someone.
commonMistakes.correction: Knowledge and control are usually distributed across designers, operators, and deployers — the problem of many hands — so responsibility must be traced through all of them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating bias in automated systems as always deliberate prejudice by programmers.
commonMistakes.correction: NIST distinguishes statistical, human, and systemic bias, and much of it enters through data and institutional history without anyone intending it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming one country's rules settle the ethics of a technology everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: There is no uniformly applied international approach to questions like measuring bias, and regulation generally lags behind technology.

compareContrast.distinction: Technology ethics is a domain of applied ethics focused on the design, development, and use of technologies; applied ethics supplies the general method (question, facts, considerations, alternatives) that the domain uses.

Contested positions: the thesis holds that technologies incorporate no values, while the critique (Winner; value-sensitive design) holds that artifacts embody power, authority, and the values of their design and deployment.
Statistical bias comes from patterns in large-scale datasets, while systemic (institutional or historical) bias is rooted in institutional norms, practices, and history that the system reproduces.
Looking for a single responsible individual versus recognizing that knowledge and control are distributed across many actors, which complicates individual ascription of responsibility.

keyTakeaway: Technologies are not value-neutral: they embody values, produce unintended consequences, and distribute responsibility across many actors, so ethical reflection belongs at every stage of design, use, and governance.

questionBank.prompt: Which claim is associated with Langdon Winner's phrase 'artifacts have politics'?
options: Some technologies embody specific forms of power and authority, or are strongly compatible with certain social and political relations.
Technologies are morally neutral until people misuse them.
Political questions about technology should be left to engineers alone.
Only governments, never designers, shape what technologies mean.
questionBank.explanation: Winner's claim is that artifacts can embody power and authority or favor certain social and political arrangements, so neutrality cannot be assumed; the other options assert neutrality, defer the question, or deny designers any role.

questionBank.prompt: According to the Collingridge dilemma, why is society's control over technological development difficult?
options: Early on, consequences are easy to predict, but no one has the authority to act.
Early on there is more control but less knowledge of consequences, while later knowledge grows but control shrinks as the technology becomes entrenched.
Regulators always know exactly what will happen once a technology becomes widespread.
The cost of changing a technology is always lowest after it has been widely adopted.
questionBank.explanation: The dilemma is that early control is high while prediction is poor, and later prediction improves while control declines because the technology is embedded and interests are invested; the other options reverse the timing or the costs.
questionBank.skill: Stating the Collingridge dilemma

questionBank.prompt: A university's automated admissions-review flag identifies applicants from one region far more often than others, and the skew tracks the institution's own past admissions practices and records. Which NIST bias category best describes this pattern?
options: Statistical bias, because the system's dataset contains patterns that skew results.
Human bias, because a programmer chose the variables.
Systemic bias, because the skew reflects institutional norms, practices, and history embedded in the records.
No bias, because the system only follows the data it was given.
questionBank.explanation: NIST defines systemic bias, also called institutional or historical bias, as bias rooted in institutional norms, practices, and history; the scenario points to the institution's own practices and records, not merely dataset patterns or a programmer's choice.
questionBank.skill: Applying the statistical/human/systemic bias taxonomy to a case

questionBank.prompt: A delivery robot malfunctions and injures a pedestrian. Investigators find the harm resulted from a design flaw, a data error, and a deployer's decision to skip safety testing. Why is assigning responsibility for the harm difficult?
options: Because only the robot itself can be blamed for its actions.
Because the harm was an accident, and accidents are never anyone's responsibility.
Because responsibility always rests with whichever person pressed the final button.
Because knowledge and control were distributed across many actors — the problem of many hands.
questionBank.explanation: The problem of many hands names the difficulty of assigning individual responsibility when knowledge and control are spread across designers, operators, and deployers; the other options blame the machine, dismiss accidents, or single out one actor arbitrarily.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing distributed responsibility for harm from an automated system

questionBank.prompt: An app collects location data and asks users to tap 'I agree' on a long terms-of-service screen; most users click through quickly. According to the privacy literature, why is consent alone considered an imperfect protection for personal data?
options: Because consent requests interfere with task flows and users routinely click them away, leaving collectors with power over data subjects.
Because laws prohibit companies from ever requesting consent.
Because consent is unnecessary once data has been collected.
Because consent permanently transfers full control of the data to the data subject.
questionBank.explanation: The literature documents that consent requests often interrupt users and are simply clicked away, so consent does not reliably give individuals control; the other options misstate the law, the purpose of consent, and its effect.

title: Environmental Ethics
in30Seconds: Environmental ethics is the philosophical study of human obligations regarding the natural world. It asks whether nature matters only because it serves human ends, or also for its own sake, and who counts morally: people alone, individual organisms, or entire ecosystems. Landmark views — Leopold's land ethic, Carson's warnings about pesticides, Naess's deep ecology — frame these questions. The field also asks what we owe future generations, and how the burdens of environmental change should be shared.
whyItMatters: Nearly every environmental decision — a wetland saved or drained, an energy source chosen, a resource used or conserved — carries a moral question beneath the factual one. Environmental ethics supplies the tools to say what that question is and to compare the reasons people give for different answers. It matters academically as one of the liveliest areas of applied philosophy, practically because citizens, professionals, and policymakers face these choices constantly, and educationally because it trains students to keep values, facts, and interests distinct instead of letting them blur together.
learningObjectives: Define environmental ethics as the philosophical study of human obligations regarding the natural world.
Distinguish anthropocentrism, biocentrism, and ecocentrism, and attribute landmark statements to their authors (Leopold's land ethic, Naess's deep ecology).
Explain the distinction between instrumental and intrinsic value and apply it to cases involving nature.
Describe Silent Spring's documented role in raising public concern about pesticides and its place in the policy history leading to the 1972 DDT cancellation order.
Explain the Brundtland Report's definition of sustainable development and identify intergenerational justice as a contested area.
Distinguish ethical questions about climate responsibility and burden-sharing from climate science questions.

collegeVersion.heading: What environmental ethics studies
collegeVersion.body: Environmental ethics is the discipline in philosophy that studies the moral relationship of human beings to the environment, and the value and moral status of the environment and its non-human contents. Although thinkers had reflected on nature and human duty for centuries, environmental ethics emerged as a distinct academic discipline in the 1970s, after a decade of growing public awareness of pollution, resource use, and population growth. The field asks two questions that are easy to run together: what duties do human beings have with respect to the natural world, and why do we have them? The second question usually has to be answered first, because different answers generate different ethics. If the reason to protect a forest is that people need it, the resulting obligations look different from the obligations that follow if the forest matters for its own sake.

collegeVersion.heading: Value and moral standing: three families of views
collegeVersion.body: A central distinction in environmental ethics is between instrumental and intrinsic value. Instrumental value is the value something has as a means to further ends; intrinsic value is the value something has as an end in itself, regardless of its usefulness. A wetland has instrumental value if it filters water that people drink; whether it also has value in its own right is what separates the major positions. Anthropocentrism — human-centeredness — is the traditional view in much Western philosophy: moral standing belongs to human beings, and nature is valuable chiefly as a means to human ends. William Baxter's People or Penguins (1974) defends an unapologetically anthropocentric environmental ethic: pollution matters because of how it affects people. Biocentrism extends moral standing to all individual living organisms. Paul Taylor argued that every living thing is a teleological center of life with a good of its own that deserves moral respect, and that all such individuals have equal intrinsic value. Ecocentrism extends moral standing to holistic entities such as rivers, species, and ecosystems — the direction classically associated with Aldo Leopold's land ethic, which treats the biotic community itself as the object of ethical concern. These families are contested, and philosophers within each disagree about details; the map matters because it shows what is at stake: who counts, and why.

collegeVersion.heading: Landmark figures and texts
collegeVersion.body: Aldo Leopold, a forester and ecologist, argued in A Sand County Almanac (1949) that ethics should be extended to the land. Its central statement: "A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise." Leopold himself offered no systematic ethical theory to support the land ethic, which later philosophers treated as a challenge to be met. Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) drew wide attention to the dangers of the commercial pesticides then in common use, such as DDT. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency records that its publication stimulated widespread public concern over improper pesticide use and the need for better controls, and in 1972 the agency issued a cancellation order for DDT based on its adverse environmental effects. Carson's book did not act alone — regulators had already begun acting in the 1950s and 1960s — but it is the best-documented catalyst of public concern. Arne Naess, a Norwegian philosopher, coined the term "deep ecology" in 1973, contrasting it with what he called the shallow ecology movement, focused on pollution and resource depletion for human benefit. Deep ecology endorses biospheric egalitarianism: all living things have value in their own right, independent of their usefulness to others, and humans should understand themselves as parts of, not separate from, the natural world.

collegeVersion.heading: Sustainability, intergenerational justice, and climate ethics
collegeVersion.body: The Brundtland Report, Our Common Future (1987), defined sustainable development as development "that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs." The definition raises questions it does not settle. Is it acceptable to replace natural resources with human-made substitutes? Weak sustainability says yes, provided the substitutes function equivalently; strong sustainability says no — a critical stock of natural systems must be preserved. And whether present generations genuinely owe duties to people who do not yet exist is itself contested; philosophers debate problems such as the non-identity problem, which asks how actions that determine who will exist can be said to harm those future people. Climate change raises the same family of questions. Climate ethics asks who is responsible for greenhouse gas emissions and how the costs of mitigation and adaptation should be shared — between countries, industries, and generations. Because emissions come from countless dispersed agents and no single global institution coordinates them, philosophers disagree about how responsibility should be assigned and burdens divided. Those are ethical debates; the scientific facts about climate change belong to the earth and space sciences. Environmental ethics supplies the question "what do we owe, and to whom," not the measurements.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies human beings' moral obligations regarding the natural world and the moral standing of its non-human contents.
Human-centeredness: the ethical view that only human beings have moral standing in their own right, so nature matters mainly as a means to human ends.
The view that all individual living organisms have moral standing and value in their own right, as in Paul Taylor's teleological-center-of-life account.
The view that ecological wholes — species, ecosystems, rivers, the biotic community — have moral standing, as in Leopold's land ethic.
The value something has as a means to further ends, such as a forest's timber or a wetland's water filtration.
The value something has as an end in itself, independent of its usefulness to anyone.
Aldo Leopold's proposal, in A Sand County Almanac (1949), to extend ethics to the land and the biotic community.
The position associated with Arne Naess that all living things have value in their own right and that humans are parts of, not separate from, the natural world.
Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; the Brundtland Report's definition.
Fairness in the distribution of benefits and burdens across generations, including contested duties owed by present to future people.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Environmental ethics is about one question: what do we owe the natural world, and why? Some people answer "because nature helps us" — that is anthropocentric thinking. Others answer "because living things matter on their own" — biocentrism. Still others answer "because whole systems, like forests, rivers, and species, matter" — ecocentrism. None of these is just a feeling; each is a reasoned position with famous defenders. The field also asks about time: do we owe anything to people who will live after us? And it asks about sharing: when the environment changes, who should carry the costs? You do not need to pick a side to study it. You need to be able to say what each side claims and what would count as evidence for or against it.
eli10.analogy: Think of a family deciding what to do with a large old tree in the yard. One person values it for the shade it gives the house — that is instrumental value. Another values it because it is a living thing with a life of its own — biocentric reasoning. A third values it as part of the neighborhood's network of trees and wildlife — ecocentric reasoning. The same tree, three different accounts of why it matters. Environmental ethics is that family conversation, slowed down, with the reasons made visible and compared.
eli10.analogyLimits: The family analogy can make the views sound like tastes, as if any answer is fine. In philosophy, these positions are argued for and against with reasons, evidence, and counterexamples, and they can conflict in ways a family conversation need not resolve. Also, a yard tree is present and visible, while much environmental ethics concerns distant people and large systems, which the analogy hides.

workedExample: A small town must decide whether to allow a construction company to drain a wetland to build a parking lot near a shopping center. The main views frame the decision differently. An anthropocentric analysis asks what the wetland does for people — flood protection, clean water, recreation — and whether the parking lot's benefits outweigh those. A biocentric analysis asks whether the plants and animals living there have goods of their own that draining would destroy. An ecocentric analysis asks what draining does to the wetland as a system and to the species and processes that depend on it. A complete discussion also looks forward: does the decision leave the town's children with options the town itself enjoyed? The facts — flood risk, species present, construction costs — are the same for everyone; the moral questions differ.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating environmental ethics as a debate about facts.
commonMistakes.correction: Science tells us what is happening — pollution levels, species counts, climate trends; ethics asks what we owe and to whom. Mixing the two turns a values question into a data question, and vice versa.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using 'anthropocentrism' to mean 'caring about the environment at all.'
commonMistakes.correction: Anthropocentrism names a specific position: only human beings have moral standing in their own right. A person can care deeply about nature while holding that view.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating deep ecology as just another word for conservation.
commonMistakes.correction: Deep ecology is a specific philosophical position associated with Arne Naess — all living things have value in their own right and humans are part of nature — not a label for any pro-environment stance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing instrumental and intrinsic value.
commonMistakes.correction: Instrumental value is value as a means to an end; intrinsic value is value as an end in itself. A thing can have both: a forest can be useful timber and valuable for its own sake.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming sustainability is one settled idea.
commonMistakes.correction: Sustainability is contested: weak and strong versions disagree about whether natural resources can be replaced by human-made equivalents, and duties to future generations are debated.

compareContrast.distinction: Grants moral standing to human beings only versus granting it to every individual living organism.
Value as a means to further ends versus value as an end in itself, regardless of usefulness.
Allows natural capital to be replaced by equivalent human-made capital versus insists a critical stock of natural systems be preserved.

keyTakeaway: Environmental ethics asks what we owe the natural world and to whom: people alone, individual organisms, ecological wholes, or future generations. Its landmark voices — Leopold, Carson, Naess — frame questions the discipline still argues about, and none of those questions is settled.

questionBank.prompt: In environmental ethics, what does 'anthropocentrism' name?
options: A human-centered approach that grants moral standing primarily or solely to human beings.
The view that every individual living organism has equal moral standing.
The view that ecological wholes such as species and ecosystems have moral standing.
A method for calculating the economic value of ecosystem services.
questionBank.explanation: Anthropocentrism literally means human-centeredness; in environmental ethics it names the view that only human beings have moral standing in their own right, so nature matters mainly as a means to human ends. Option B describes biocentrism, C describes ecocentrism, and D describes economic valuation rather than a position on moral standing.
questionBank.skill: Defining anthropocentrism and distinguishing it from biocentrism and ecocentrism

questionBank.prompt: A philosopher says a wetland has value 'as an end in itself, regardless of its usefulness to anyone.' Which distinction is she drawing on?
options: The distinction between anthropocentrism and ecocentrism.
The distinction between weak and strong sustainability.
The distinction between intrinsic and instrumental value.
The distinction between shallow and deep ecology.
questionBank.explanation: Valuing something as an end in itself is intrinsic value, as opposed to instrumental value, which is value as a means to further ends — so option C is the distinction being used. The other pairs are real distinctions in environmental ethics, but none of them concerns the source of value named in the question.
questionBank.skill: Applying the intrinsic-versus-instrumental value distinction

questionBank.prompt: A city planner argues that a forest should be protected because it cleans the air residents breathe and stores water the city uses. Which approach does this reasoning exemplify?
options: Biocentrism, because it treats the forest's organisms as having goods of their own.
Anthropocentrism, because it justifies protection through benefits to human beings.
Ecocentrism, because it treats the forest as a whole system with moral standing.
Deep ecology, because it denies that nature has value only for humans.
questionBank.explanation: The argument appeals to what the forest does for people — clean air and stored water — which is anthropocentric reasoning that values nature instrumentally. Option A misreads the reasoning as valuing organisms for their own sake, C misreads it as valuing the system itself, and D states the opposite of the argument's human-benefit framing.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the value framework at work in an ordinary case

questionBank.prompt: The Brundtland Report defines sustainable development as development that 'meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.' Why does this definition raise ethical questions rather than settle them?
options: Because the report is a treaty that carries no moral weight.
Because future generations cannot be named individually, so they cannot have interests.
Because it describes present economic growth and ignores the environment entirely.
Because it leaves open contested matters — what counts as a need, and how present and future interests should be weighed — which philosophers continue to debate.
questionBank.explanation: The definition gives a direction but not a decision procedure: what counts as a need and how present and future well-being should be weighed are exactly the contested questions in sustainability and intergenerational justice, so option D is correct. Options A, B, and C misstate the report's status, the grounds on which future people's interests are debated, and the report's environmental content.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing why a standard definition leaves normative questions open

questionBank.prompt: Residents of a coastal town disagree about how to respond to flooding linked to changing climate. Which question belongs to environmental ethics rather than to climate science?
options: How much has sea level risen near the town in the past decade?
Who should bear the costs of reducing emissions and adapting — residents, industry, or future generations?
Which storm patterns are expected in the region over the next decade?
Which engineering options would most effectively reduce flood risk?
questionBank.explanation: Who should carry the costs, and how burdens should be shared across people and generations, is a question of responsibility and justice — the subject of climate ethics. Options A and C are empirical climate-science questions, and D is an engineering question; all three are factual rather than moral.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing ethical questions from scientific and technical ones in a climate case

title: AI Ethics
in30Seconds: AI ethics is the branch of applied ethics that studies moral questions raised by artificial intelligence: systems that decide, recommend, or predict. Its main issue clusters include fairness and bias, opacity and explainability, accountability for harms, privacy and surveillance, safety and alignment, and effects on work. Since about 2015, governments, companies, and professional bodies have published many AI ethics principles, but most are voluntary. Whether principles can change practice, and who should enforce them, is itself an open debate.
whyItMatters: Automated systems already influence who gets a loan, a job interview, a medical recommendation, or a housing application. These are morally significant decisions, and the systems behind them can reproduce bias, resist explanation, and spread responsibility across many actors. Studying AI ethics builds the habit of asking who is affected, what a system's limits are, and who answers for outcomes. It also clarifies why written principles alone do not settle the matter: implementation, enforcement, and power decide whether values become practice.
learningObjectives: Define AI ethics as the field of applied ethics examining moral questions raised by artificial intelligence systems.
Explain how automated systems can reproduce or amplify bias in training data and design.
Distinguish transparency from explainability and describe the debate over whether opaque decisions are ever acceptable.
Analyze the many-hands problem of allocating responsibility when AI systems cause harm.
Describe the landscape of AI ethics principles and evaluate the limits of principle-based approaches.
Summarize the main positions in debates about AI safety and labor effects without adjudicating between them.

collegeVersion.heading: What AI ethics is
collegeVersion.body: AI ethics is the branch of applied ethics that examines moral questions raised by the design, deployment, and use of artificial intelligence. It is useful to treat AI systems as decision systems: they take in data and produce outputs that recommend, rank, or decide, and those outputs can affect real people. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy observes that the field is difficult because it requires normative ethics, an understanding of the technologies, and expertise in the many areas of social impact. The field is commonly divided into short-term questions about current systems, such as bias, privacy, and accountability, and long-term questions about future systems, such as safety and superintelligence. Scholars also caution that discussion should not be dominated by imagined technology rather than the systems that actually exist.

collegeVersion.heading: Fairness, bias, and the quality of data
collegeVersion.body: Automated systems can reproduce or amplify bias. NIST, the U.S. standards agency, reports that biases are endemic across technology processes and can lead to harmful impacts regardless of intent, and that AI can newly introduce or amplify biases. Bias can enter at several points: through the training data, when a dataset under-represents a group or encodes past discrimination; through design choices, such as which features a system uses or how success is defined; and through feedback, when a system's own outputs shape the future data it receives. Documented cases reported in the research literature include gender bias in hiring tools, racial disparities in credit and parole risk assessments, and facial recognition systems performing worse on darker skin tones. Remedies are not purely technical: NIST identifies systemic, statistical, and human categories of bias, and philosophers note that competing mathematical definitions of fairness are hard to reconcile.

collegeVersion.heading: Opacity, explainability, and the trade-off debate
collegeVersion.body: Many AI systems are opaque, or black boxes: the person affected by a decision, such as a denied loan or a rejected application, often cannot know how the output was produced, and with some machine-learning systems even the programmers do not fully know which patterns in the data drove the result. The ACM identifies three sources of opacity: technical, when an algorithm does not lend itself to easy explanation; economic, when transparency is costly or would compromise trade secrets; and social, when revealing inputs would violate privacy expectations. Some ethicists argue that explainability is a basic requirement, because decisions about important parts of people's lives should be justifiable to them. Others argue that what matters is whether machine decisions are well calibrated, and that a human-style explanation may not be what is actually needed. Explainable AI is now a significant technical field, but whether explanation, justification, or calibration should be the goal remains an open debate.

collegeVersion.heading: Accountability, privacy, and surveillance
collegeVersion.body: When an automated system harms someone, who answers? Responsibility is distributed across many actors, including data collectors, developers, deployers, users, and regulators. Philosophers have discussed a responsibility gap: in some cases neither the machine nor any individual human appears clearly responsible for the harm. Proposed remedies include keeping humans in the loop or in meaningful control, though whether that genuinely solves the allocation problem is debated, and some argue the difficulty is only temporary confusion about how to allocate responsibility among humans. Privacy is a related cluster. AI depends on large amounts of personal data, and surveillance can be conducted by states, companies, and individuals; the encyclopedia literature describes regulation as slow to respond to these changes.

collegeVersion.heading: Safety, work, and the limits of principles
collegeVersion.body: Technical AI safety, sometimes called alignment, is an active research area closely related to AI ethics but not identical to it; its definitions and goals are contested, so this lesson reports the debate rather than endorsing any position. On labor, responses to automation range from alarmed to neutral to optimistic. Historical experience shows that productivity gains have not necessarily meant net job loss, though job polarization, growth at the high- and low-skill ends of the labor market with pressure on mid-skill jobs, is a documented pattern. Since roughly 2015 to 2020, governments, the European Union, companies, and professional associations have published many sets of AI ethics principles. A comparative review of 84 such sets found strong convergence on transparency, justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility, and privacy. Yet most of these documents are voluntary, and critics describe some as ethics washing or toothless, while defenders treat them as useful work in progress. Implementation, enforcement, and power remain the central limits of principle-based approaches, which is why some jurisdictions, such as the EU with its AI Act, have begun to move toward binding regulation.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of applied ethics that examines moral questions raised by the design, deployment, and use of artificial intelligence systems.
Systematic unfairness in an automated system's outputs, which can enter through training data, design choices, or feedback effects.
The condition in which the reasons for an AI system's output cannot be understood by the people affected, and sometimes not even by its developers; also called the black box problem.
The quality of an AI system's decisions being describable in terms humans can understand, proposed by some ethicists as a requirement for acceptable automated decision-making.
The situation, discussed by philosophers, in which neither the machine nor any individual human appears clearly responsible for an AI-related harm.
A contested term for the research goal of making AI systems' behavior match human values and intentions; an active area of technical AI safety.
The use of machines and software to perform tasks previously done by humans, with debated consequences for employment and the distribution of wealth.
A critical term for using ethical language or guidelines to create an appearance of responsibility without meaningful change in practice.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: AI ethics is the study of right and wrong in machines that decide things for us. A computer program that approves loans, ranks job applicants, or suggests medical treatments can be helpful, and it can also carry forward old unfairness without meaning to. The problems fall into a few big questions. Is the system treating everyone fairly, or just copying the bias in its data? Can anyone explain why it made its decision? If something goes wrong, who is responsible? What happens to privacy and jobs as these systems spread? Around the world, organizations have written down principles for ethical AI: be transparent, be fair, be accountable. But a principle is a promise, not a rule with teeth. Most of these documents are voluntary, so a central question in AI ethics is how to turn good intentions into practice that is actually checked and enforced.
eli10.analogy: Think of an AI system as a very fast copy machine. It does not create the document from nothing; it reproduces whatever is in the original. If the original pages, the training data, contain smudges and missing lines, the copies will contain them too, only faster and in bulk. What looks like a neutral machine is really reproducing the quality of what it was given.
eli10.analogyLimits: A copy machine copies exactly, while an AI system learns patterns. That means it can do more than copy: it can amplify a small pattern into a large one, or find patterns the data did not obviously contain. So the machine is not passive, and fixing the input is only part of the solution.

workedExample: Consider a hypothetical city that replaces its paper rental-application screening with an automated system trained on a decade of past approvals. The goal is speed and consistency, but the old records reflect years of informal practices, including agents steering applicants of some backgrounds toward certain buildings. The new system learns patterns from that biased past. An applicant denied by the system cannot get a clear reason, because the model's outputs are opaque even to the vendor's engineers. The city council then asks who is responsible if the system discriminates: the data provider, the vendor, the agency that deployed it, or the official who approved it. The case shows three clusters working together: bias in data, opacity in decisions, and a responsibility gap among many hands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming machines are neutral and objective because they are computers.
commonMistakes.correction: Bias can enter through training data and design choices, and harmful outcomes can occur regardless of intent; a system can reproduce or amplify patterns in what it was given.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming transparency always fixes everything, or that opacity is always wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: The trade-off is debated: transparency has costs such as trade secrets and privacy, and some ethicists argue well-calibrated decisions matter more than explanations.

commonMistakes.mistake: Blaming the AI itself as if it were a moral agent.
commonMistakes.correction: In the standard view, machines are not moral agents; responsibility is distributed among the humans and institutions that collect data, build, deploy, and regulate the system.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating published AI ethics principles as enforceable law.
commonMistakes.correction: Most principles are voluntary and non-binding; critics call them ethics washing or toothless, and enforcement and implementation are open problems.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating contested long-term scenarios as settled facts.
commonMistakes.correction: Safety and alignment are active research areas with contested definitions; the honest move is to report the debate and attribute positions.

compareContrast.distinction: AI ethics focuses on systems that decide, recommend, or predict, and their fairness, opacity, and accountability; technology ethics covers the broader moral questions of technology as a whole, including environmental and professional concerns.
Transparency is about access to how a system works, while explainability is about whether its specific decisions can be understood and justified to those affected.
Principles are aspirational commitments with weak enforcement, while regulation such as the EU AI Act carries legal obligations, though its effectiveness is debated.

keyTakeaway: AI ethics examines fairness, bias, opacity, accountability, privacy, safety, and the labor effects of automated systems; most current AI ethics principles are voluntary, so implementation, enforcement, and power remain open, contested questions.

questionBank.prompt: In AI ethics, the 'black box problem' refers to which situation?
options: An AI system's decisions cannot be understood by the people affected, and sometimes not even by its developers.
An AI system is physically stored in a secure facility that the public cannot enter.
An AI system makes errors only when its training data contain obvious mistakes.
An AI system refuses to process requests from users it does not recognize.
questionBank.explanation: The black box problem is opacity: with many machine-learning systems, neither the affected people nor the programmers can fully see which patterns in the data produced a given output. The other options describe physical security, data quality, and access control, not opacity.
questionBank.skill: Recalls the definition of opacity in AI ethics

questionBank.prompt: According to a comparative review of 84 sets of AI ethics guidelines, which statement best describes the findings?
options: The guidelines disagreed so completely that no shared principles could be identified.
The guidelines agreed that AI systems should never make decisions affecting people.
The guidelines converged strongly on principles such as transparency, justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility, and privacy.
The guidelines required all AI systems to run without any human oversight.
questionBank.explanation: The comparative review by Jobin and colleagues found strong convergence across 84 guideline sets on principles including transparency, justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility, and privacy. The other options misstate the findings: convergence existed, and the guidelines neither banned decisions nor required full automation.
questionBank.skill: Interprets empirical findings about AI ethics guideline convergence

questionBank.prompt: A company trains its hiring screener on decades of its own past hiring records, which reflect old patterns of favoring certain applicant backgrounds, and the screener now ranks applicants accordingly. Which ethical concern does this best illustrate?
options: Opacity, because the screener's output is always wrong.
Alignment, because the screener's goals differ from the company's stated mission.
Accountability, because no one at the company knows the screener exists.
Bias, because the system can reproduce historical patterns present in its training data.
questionBank.explanation: This is the classic training-data bias case: a system trained on data that encode past discrimination can codify and automate that history. Opacity, alignment, and accountability are genuine concerns in general, but the scenario as described is specifically about bias entering through the data.
questionBank.skill: Applies the bias concept to a concrete automated-decision scenario

questionBank.prompt: Why do some philosophers describe a 'responsibility gap' for harms caused by AI systems?
options: Because AI systems are legal persons that cannot be sued.
Because responsibility is spread across many actors, such as data collectors, developers, deployers, and users, so neither the machine nor any single human may be clearly responsible.
Because courts have ruled that machines are never responsible for their actions.
Because the designers of AI systems are always anonymous employees.
questionBank.explanation: The responsibility gap arises when responsibility is diffused across many hands: neither the machine nor any individual human is clearly answerable for a harm. The other options misstate the legal and factual picture: AI systems are not legal persons, and no such blanket court ruling exists.
questionBank.skill: Explains the many-hands problem of responsibility allocation

questionBank.prompt: An organization publishes a voluntary AI ethics code promising fairness and transparency, then deploys a system it does not audit or explain. Critics call this 'ethics washing.' Which response best captures the debate over principle-based approaches?
options: Critics and defenders agree that voluntary principles have no effect whatsoever on practice.
Defenders argue that transparency and fairness are mathematically guaranteed by any ethics code.
Critics say principles can be toothless or used for public relations, while defenders treat them as useful work in progress; enforcement and implementation remain open questions.
The debate is settled: principles are always more effective than binding regulation.
questionBank.explanation: The literature reports the full range: some scholars call principles meaningless, toothless, or ethics washing, while others defend them as work in progress toward operationalization, with enforcement and power as the recognized limits. The other options assert settled or extreme positions the debate does not support.
questionBank.skill: Analyzes the contested value of principle-based AI ethics
