title: Social Media
in30Seconds: Social media are internet-based platforms built on user-generated content: people post text, images, and video, maintain profiles, and connect through followers, friends, and groups. Because design shapes use, the visible buttons — share, like, comment, follow — steer how people participate, and engagement signals help algorithms rank what appears in each feed. Most services are free to use and funded by advertising built on user data. Their effects on attention, well-being, and public debate remain contested research questions.
whyItMatters: Social media are where many people now encounter culture, news, and each other, so understanding how platforms work — what content they show, why they show it, and who pays for them — is basic to media literacy. The same concepts apply to any networked service: the feed is a curated view, not a neutral mirror, and engagement metrics are design choices with consequences. Knowing the difference between an algorithm's ranking and a complete record lets you interpret what you see without assuming conspiracy. And because effects on attention, well-being, and political debate are genuinely contested, a careful student can evaluate the research instead of repeating slogans.
learningObjectives: Define social media as internet-based services built on user-generated content, user-created profiles, and networks of connections.
Identify the core affordances of sharing, liking, commenting, and following, and explain how design choices shape the way people use a platform.
Explain how engagement-based algorithms rank content and why a feed is a curated view rather than a complete record.
Describe the ad-funded economics of free social media services and the role of user data in targeting.
Analyze contested research on echo chambers, filter bubbles, polarization, misinformation, attention, and well-being, attributing findings to the studies reported in the sources.
Distinguish platform rules, moderation, and the legal frameworks that shape who decides what stays online.

collegeVersion.heading: Platforms, profiles, and user-generated content
collegeVersion.body: Social media are internet-based services whose content comes largely from users rather than professional staff. A 2015 review summarized in the Wikipedia article on social media identifies four defining features: Web 2.0 internet-based applications; user-generated content such as posts, photos, and videos; user-created self profiles; and social networks formed by connections between profiles. The University of Minnesota open textbook makes the same basic distinction: social media is the blanket term for person-to-person connections on the Internet, unlike television, radio, or newspapers, and "Web 2.0" does not name a new version of the web but rather the increased focus on user-generated content and social interaction. A platform is therefore not a broadcaster with a fixed audience but an environment where the audience produces much of what appears, and where each user's connections determine part of what they see.

collegeVersion.heading: Affordances: how design shapes participation
collegeVersion.body: Platforms do not merely host content; their interfaces invite specific actions. Sharing, liking, commenting, and following are affordances — possible actions made visible and convenient by design — and different designs support different uses. A service built around following accounts and short posts encourages rapid scanning of many voices, while a profile-based network organized around mutual "friends" supports maintaining a personal circle. Engagement metrics such as likes, comments, shares, and views make audience response visible and countable, turning audience reaction into a signal that both users and software can act on. The open textbook notes that a character limit once described as a constraint proved useful to time-strapped users, showing that design can shape a medium's character. Before asking what a platform "does to" people, describe what its interface invites them to do.

collegeVersion.heading: Algorithmic feeds and virality
collegeVersion.body: Many services rank posts with algorithms rather than showing everything in upload order. The Wikipedia article on social media reports that algorithms tracking user engagement to prioritize what is shown tend to favor content that spurs strong reactions, which critics note can elevate partisan or inflammatory material. The feed a user sees is therefore a curated view produced by ranking software — a selection based on predicted engagement, recency, and past behavior — not a complete record of everything posted. Virality is the related phenomenon of content spreading from person to person without direction from a mainstream source; the open textbook defines "gone viral" that way, and the Wikipedia article adds that virality is not guaranteed: few posts make the transition. Internet memes — catchphrases, images, or videos that replicate across networks — are one product of this spread, and marketers attempt to engineer it through viral campaigns with famously unpredictable results.

collegeVersion.heading: The economics of 'free'
collegeVersion.body: Most social media services are free to users, and that free access is funded by advertising. The open textbook's commerce section explains the model: services offer free use while selling the ability to reach audiences, and marketers can target advertising using information users provide — age, location, interests — along with behavior such as the pages and posts a user engages with. The textbook frames the privacy question in economic terms: much of the debate is about how much information users are willing to share with advertisers. Attention, in this model, is the product: platforms sell access to attention, and engagement data makes that attention more valuable. This does not make every platform motive sinister; it makes the business model a structural fact of the environment. When a feed places an ad between posts, the placement is not an accident but the designed intersection of free service, user data, and advertiser demand.

collegeVersion.heading: Contested effects: echo chambers, polarization, well-being
collegeVersion.body: Research on social media's effects is genuinely contested. The filter bubble concept — popularized by Eli Pariser around 2010 — holds that personalized algorithms enclose users in information that reinforces existing beliefs, yet the Wikipedia article on filter bubbles states plainly that conflicting reports exist about the extent of personalized filtering and that various studies have produced inconclusive results. A Wharton study of music recommendations found filters could create commonality rather than fragmentation, and an experiment that manipulated a platform's algorithm found little change in participants' opinions. On well-being, the open textbook presents the 1998 "Internet paradox" study suggesting heavy Internet use correlated with loneliness, alongside the critique that it lacked a control group and later research (Ellison, Steinfield, and Lampe, 2007) finding positive associations with social capital. Polarization and misinformation research likewise divides between critics who point to engagement-driven amplification and studies emphasizing user choice. All of these should be attributed and weighed, not asserted as settled fact.

collegeVersion.heading: Moderation and platform governance
collegeVersion.body: Platforms are not neutral conduits; they set rules for what may be posted and enforce them. Content moderation is the systematic review, labeling, or removal of user contributions that a platform's rules or the law prohibit, and major platforms combine automated tools, user reporting, and human review. In the United States, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 shields platforms from liability for content authored by third parties, which is why a platform can remove posts without being treated as their publisher. In the European Union, the Digital Services Act, enacted in 2022, requires very large platforms to remove illegal content and to assess and reduce risks to minors and fundamental rights. Who decides what stays online — platforms, governments, or users — is an open debate: some argue moderation is too aggressive and opaque, others that it is too lax. The analytic task is to describe the rules and their consequences, not to take sides by default.

vocabulary.definition: Internet-based services where users generate content, maintain profiles, and connect through networks of followers, friends, or groups.
Text, images, video, and other material created and published by users rather than by a platform's staff or professional producers.
A user-created public or semi-public identity page on a service, typically carrying a name, image, and activity history.
A possible action made available and encouraged by a design, such as a like button or a share icon.
Counts and signals such as likes, comments, shares, and views that record how audiences respond to content.
A personalized content stream in which software ranks and orders posts using signals such as predicted engagement, recency, and past behavior.
The spread of a post from person to person without direction from a mainstream source; few posts achieve it.
The contested idea that personalized algorithms enclose users in information that reinforces existing beliefs while hiding conflicting views.
A social setting, online or offline, in which people encounter mainly information and opinions that agree with their own.
The systematic review, labeling, or removal of user contributions to enforce a platform's rules or the law.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Social media are places online where the people using them make the content. You post a photo, follow people you know, and scroll a feed that someone — or rather, something — has arranged for you. The buttons you see matter: a like button invites quick approval, a comment box invites conversation, a share button invites spreading things further. Most of these sites are free, which is possible because advertising pays for them, and ads are aimed using information about what you do and like. The feed you see is not everything that happened; it is a selection made by ranking software that favors what it predicts you will engage with. Researchers disagree about how much this shapes attention, mood, and politics, so the honest answer is that the effects are real questions, not settled facts.
eli10.analogy: Think of a town square where anyone can put up a poster, and a town manager decides which posters get hung at eye level near the fountain because they get the most reactions. Your view of the square is real, but it is arranged, not accidental.
eli10.analogyLimits: The square has one visible order for everyone; feeds are personal, built for each user from their own history. A town manager also acts openly, while ranking criteria are usually invisible, and the square does not collect your past visits to decide what you see next. A real platform also sets rules for what can be posted at all, which the square does not.

workedExample: A student opens a social app and sees three posts: a dance video with 40,000 likes, a friend's photo with two comments, and a community notice about a free concert. The app ranks by predicted engagement, so the video leads the feed. The student then follows the concert organizer and likes two posts about local music; within a week, similar posts appear more often, and an ad for a local instrument shop appears between them. Tracing the example: the visible order was produced by ranking software, the follow and likes changed later predictions, and the ad reflects the ad-funded model. None of this requires the app to be 'manipulative'; it is the designed behavior of the system, and analyzing it means naming each element — engagement ranking, personalization, advertising — separately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling the feed 'everything that was posted.'
commonMistakes.correction: The feed is a ranked selection built by software; content exists that users never see, so treat the visible stream as a curated view rather than a complete record.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating contested effects as settled fact.
commonMistakes.correction: Research on filter bubbles, polarization, and well-being is mixed; attribute findings to specific studies and describe the debate rather than declaring that social media 'causes' an outcome.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing 'free' with 'without a business model.'
commonMistakes.correction: Free access is funded by advertising and data; the service sells attention and targeting, so user activity is part of the product even when no money changes hands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming engagement counts equal importance or truth.
commonMistakes.correction: A high like count measures audience reaction, not accuracy or representativeness; viral reach and credibility are separate questions.

compareContrast.distinction: Broadcast media push content one-to-many from a central producer; social media are many-to-many environments where users generate the content and networks of connections shape what each person sees.
A chronological timeline shows posts in upload order; an algorithmic feed ranks posts by predicted engagement and other signals, producing a curated view instead of a complete record.

A filter bubble is the contested claim that personalization algorithms enclose users in reinforcing information; an echo chamber is the broader pattern of encountering mainly agreeing views, which can also arise from user choice and homogenous networks.

keyTakeaway: Social media are designed environments: user-generated content, engagement-driven ranking, and ad-funded economics shape what people see and do, while their effects on attention and public debate remain contested questions rather than settled facts.

questionBank.prompt: A 2015 review identifies four features as defining social media services. Which set is correct?
options: Web 2.0 applications, user-generated content, user-created profiles, and networks formed by connections between profiles
Professional editorial staff, scheduled broadcasts, printed archives, and paid subscriptions
Search engines, databases, encryption, and domain registration
Email lists, telephone directories, fax machines, and newsstands
questionBank.explanation: The 2015 review summarized in the Social media article identifies exactly those four features: Web 2.0 applications, user-generated content, user-created self profiles, and social networks formed by connections between profiles. The other options describe broadcasting, technical infrastructure, or older communication media, not social media's defining features.
questionBank.skill: Recalls the four defining features of social media services identified in a 2015 review.

questionBank.prompt: A clip spreads because users forward it to their own networks without any television, radio, or newsroom promoting it. Which term best describes what happened?
options: Broadcasting
Going viral
Pay-per-click advertising
Content moderation
questionBank.explanation: Media that spreads from person to person without direction from a mainstream source has 'gone viral,' as the open textbook defines it. Broadcasting is one-to-many transmission from a central source, and the other options concern advertising payment and content review rather than person-to-person spread.
questionBank.skill: Explains virality as person-to-person spread without direction from a mainstream source.

questionBank.prompt: An app replaces its newest-first timeline with a feed that orders posts by predicted likes, comments, and watch time. Which statement best describes the change?
options: The app now shows a complete record of every post in order of upload
The app has removed all advertising from the service
The feed is now an engagement-ranked, curated view rather than a chronological list
Users can no longer follow or unfollow other accounts
questionBank.explanation: Ranking posts by predicted engagement makes the feed a curated view produced by ranking software, not a complete chronological record, matching how engagement-based algorithms prioritize content. The other options misdescribe the change: upload order is gone, advertising is unrelated to this change, and following remains an affordance.
questionBank.skill: Applies the concept of engagement-based algorithmic ranking to a described platform redesign.

questionBank.prompt: A classmate claims that research proves personalized feeds trap every user in a filter bubble that radicalizes their opinions. Which response is most consistent with the research as reported in this lesson's sources?
options: The research is unanimous, so no further study is needed
Filter bubbles cannot exist because personalization is illegal
Algorithms never rank content, so the claim is impossible
Evidence is mixed: some studies find limited or inconclusive personalization effects, and some experiments found little change in opinion
questionBank.explanation: The Filter bubble article reports conflicting findings: some studies found the extent of personalized filtering limited or inconclusive, and an algorithm-manipulation experiment found little change in participants' opinions, so the strong claim is not supported by the reported research. The other options assert unanimity, an untrue legal claim, or a false denial that ranking exists.
questionBank.skill: Evaluates a strong causal claim about filter bubbles against contested research findings.

questionBank.prompt: In the United States, a social platform removes a user's post that its rules prohibit, and the user sues, arguing the platform should be treated as the publisher of the removed content. Which legal framework most directly shapes the outcome?
options: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which shields platforms from liability for third-party content
The Digital Services Act's risk-assessment requirements
The First Amendment requirement that platforms publish everything
Broadcast licensing rules from the Federal Communications Commission
questionBank.explanation: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) exempts internet platforms from liability for content authored by third parties, which is the framework most directly at stake when a platform moderates user posts in the United States. The Digital Services Act is EU law, the First Amendment does not require platforms to publish everything, and broadcast licensing does not govern social platforms.
questionBank.skill: Applies the US Section 230 framework to a platform-moderation dispute.

title: Media Literacy
in30Seconds: Media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication. It starts from one premise: media messages are constructed by people who make choices. A media-literate reader asks who created a message, why, for whom, with what techniques, what it omits, and how other people may read it differently. Because the habit carries into classrooms, workplaces, and civic life, it is a foundation for every other media-studies topic.
whyItMatters: Media literacy is the entry skill for every other topic in media studies: analyzing advertising, news, propaganda, or representation presupposes the habit of asking who constructed a message and why. It also works outside the classroom. Product reviews, job postings, campaign posts, and video recommendations reward the same questions, which is why NAMLE describes media literacy as empowering critical thinkers, makers, effective communicators, and active citizens. UNESCO makes the stakes concrete: critical engagement with information, safe navigation of online spaces, and resilience against mis- and disinformation are part of building trust in the information environment. The skill set is practical and civic at once.
learningObjectives: Define media literacy as the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication.
Identify the core concepts of media literacy, including construction, media language, differing audience experiences, commercial and ideological interests, and values and points of view.
Apply a standard set of analytic questions, covering creator, purpose, audience, techniques, omission, and differing interpretations, to a described media text.
Explain why media literacy matters for participation, citizenship, and resilience against misleading content.
Distinguish the analytical stance of media literacy, which is skeptical inquiry, from dismissal, which is cynicism.
Evaluate a sample media scenario using evidence from the text and its context rather than assumptions about intent or effect.

collegeVersion.heading: Media literacy is a skill set, not an attitude
collegeVersion.body: Media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication. That is the definition NAMLE, the National Association for Media Literacy Education, publishes in its Core Principles, and it is a working definition for the field: media literacy expands the idea of literacy beyond print to include moving images, sound, and digital formats, and it treats analysis and expression as two sides of the same skill. A media-literate person can find a message, take it apart, judge it against evidence, make something of their own, and do something with the result, whether that means sharing a response, correcting a misreading, or acting on what was learned. The definition matters because it makes media literacy a skill set rather than an opinion. It does not tell you which films are good or which news outlets to trust. It gives you a repeatable way of asking questions, and it demands that your answers rest on evidence. That is why media literacy education, the field devoted to teaching these skills, is described as cultivating critical thinkers, effective communicators, and active citizens rather than as training audiences to approve or reject content.

collegeVersion.heading: Five core concepts frame the analysis
collegeVersion.body: Media literacy frameworks rest on a small set of core concepts, and one of the clearest published expressions is in NAMLE's Core Principles. The first concept is construction: all media messages are built from choices about selection, arrangement, and technique, so a message is never a neutral window on reality. The second is media language: each medium communicates through its own codes and conventions. Film, for example, speaks through shots, editing, camera movement, lighting, and sound, a cinematic language with rules that filmmakers and audiences share, as the University of Arkansas open textbook puts it. The third concept is audience: different people experience the same message differently, because individuals construct meaning from their own skills, beliefs, and experiences. The fourth concept is interests: media institutions are commercial entities, and media experiences are shaped by systems of power. A studio, a platform, or a newsroom operates within economic and political arrangements, and those arrangements leave traces in what gets made. The fifth concept is viewpoint: all media messages contain values and points of view. Every message has a perspective, a context, and a purpose, whether or not the creator states them. These five concepts are not a verdict machine. NAMLE emphasizes that media analysis is evidence-based, open-ended exploration rather than a hunt for single predetermined correct readings. The concepts are starting points; the questions do the work.

collegeVersion.heading: Questions, evidence, and the boundary between skepticism and cynicism
collegeVersion.body: Putting the concepts to work means asking a short set of questions of any media text. Who created this message? For what purpose? For whom? With what techniques? What is omitted? How might other people experience it differently? Consider an original example: a three-minute film about a city's new transit line, produced by the transit authority's communications office. The creator is a public agency with an interest in ridership; the techniques include bright, handheld footage and upbeat music; the film omits the line's delays and the bus stops it replaced. A displaced resident may read the same film as promotion, while a commuter may read it as useful news. Each answer must be supported by evidence from the text and its context. This is where media literacy draws its boundary. The stance it teaches is skeptical, not cynical: skepticism withholds judgment until the evidence is in, while cynicism assumes deception in advance. NAMLE makes the point explicitly, describing media literacy education as developing skeptical, not cynical, approaches, and the organization adds that media literacy is not an anti-media movement. It raises critical questions about media and technology without condemning media as such. Nor does it replace specialized fields: advertising, news, propaganda, and representation each have their own lessons in this curriculum. Media literacy supplies the shared habit of inquiry those topics build on, and it is what makes participation in a mediated democracy possible.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication.
A constructed unit of communication, such as a film, image, post, or broadcast, examined for how it was made and what it carries.
The result of the choices, including selection, arrangement, and technique, that shape any media message.
The codes and conventions, such as framing, editing, sound, and pacing in moving images, through which a medium communicates.
The people for whom a message is made or by whom it is encountered; different audiences may construct different meanings.
The perspective and values embedded in a message, carried by a creator's choices whether stated or not.
Information, voices, or events that a message leaves out; analysis asks about these alongside what is shown.
A questioning stance that withholds judgment about a message until evidence supports a conclusion.
A stance that dismisses media messages as worthless or automatically deceptive before examining them.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Media literacy is a set of skills for dealing with anything made to communicate, like a movie, a post, an ad, or a news story. It starts from one idea: someone made this, and making means choosing. Then it asks a few plain questions. Who made it? Why? For whom? How did they try to hold your attention? What did they leave out? How might you see it differently from someone else? You do not need to find the one correct meaning. You need to look at what is actually in the message, think about how it was put together, and hold your conclusion until you have checked it.
eli10.analogy: Think of a friend telling you about a school trip. The friend chooses which details to tell, which to skip, and which order to tell them in. If you want the full picture, you listen, then ask what else happened, who else was there, and why the story was told that way.
eli10.analogyLimits: A media message is built more deliberately than an offhand story. Teams, budgets, cameras, editing, and distribution shape it, and the creator may be a company rather than a person you know. The questions still work, but the answers often need checking against other sources and other viewers' experiences.

workedExample: A three-minute video about a neighborhood renovation circulates online. It shows new benches and planters, cheerful music, and residents smiling. A media-literate analysis asks: who made it, why, for whom, with what techniques, what is omitted, and how others might read it. The city's development office produced it, judging by the logo in the opening frame; its purpose is to build support for the project; its audience is neighborhood residents and local media; its techniques include bright lighting, upbeat music, and fast cuts; it omits rent increases and construction noise; and a tenant association may read it as promotion. Each answer points to evidence in the video or its context, which keeps the analysis supported rather than assumed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing media literacy with disliking media.
commonMistakes.correction: Media literacy is analytical, not anti-media. NAMLE states explicitly that media literacy is not an anti-media movement; the questions can end in appreciation as easily as criticism.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the core concepts as a formula that decides whether a message is good or bad.
commonMistakes.correction: The concepts are starting points for inquiry, and NAMLE describes media analysis as evidence-based, open-ended exploration rather than a search for predetermined correct readings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a single correct interpretation exists for every message.
commonMistakes.correction: Different people construct different meanings from the same message, so analysis supports a reading with evidence instead of declaring the one true reading.

commonMistakes.mistake: Concluding that a creator's motive explains everything in a message.
commonMistakes.correction: Purpose and technique are separate questions. A claim about why a message was made needs evidence from the text and its context, just like a claim about what it shows.

compareContrast.distinction: Skepticism withholds judgment until evidence supports a conclusion; cynicism assumes the message is deceptive and dismisses it before examining it. NAMLE describes media literacy education as developing skeptical, not cynical, approaches.
Media literacy is the skill set an individual can practice; media literacy education is the field devoted to teaching those skills across schools, universities, libraries, and community settings.
A media message is the constructed communication itself; media language is the set of codes and conventions, such as editing and sound in moving images, used to build it.

keyTakeaway: Media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication; it is a practiced skill set of asking questions, not a stance of distrust.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best matches the definition of media literacy that NAMLE publishes?
options: The habit of distrusting everything produced by media companies
The ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication
The study of how cameras and editing software work
The practice of avoiding news and social media

questionBank.prompt: The core concept that all media messages are constructed means that every message:
options: results from choices about selection, arrangement, and technique
is fabricated and therefore false
appears spontaneously without human involvement
counts as construction only in fictional films
questionBank.explanation: Construction refers to the choices behind a message, not to falsehood: a documentary is constructed too. NAMLE's Core Principles state that all media messages are built from choices, which is why analysis examines how a message was made.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting the core concept of construction.

questionBank.prompt: A city transit authority releases a short film about a new bus route, showing bright footage of smiling riders and never mentioning the route's delays. Which of the six key questions is aimed directly at what the film leaves out?
options: How might different people experience this film differently?
What is omitted from this message?
Who created this message?
What creative techniques attract attention?
questionBank.explanation: The omission question asks what information, voices, or events a message leaves out, which is exactly what the film's silence about delays addresses. The other questions are worth asking, but they target audience, creator, and technique instead.
questionBank.skill: Applying the analytic question set to a described media text.

questionBank.prompt: Two viewers watch the same short film about a renovation project: a developer who financed it and a long-time resident whose rent increased. Which situation best fits what media literacy teaches about audiences?
options: The two viewers must form identical interpretations because the film is fixed
The film's meaning exists only in the developer's intent
The viewers may construct different meanings, because people bring different experiences and positions to the same message
The resident is required to reject the film as false
questionBank.explanation: NAMLE's Core Principles state that individuals construct personal meanings from their own skills, beliefs, and experiences, so different viewers can read the same message differently. Neither identical interpretations nor forced rejection follows from the concept.
questionBank.skill: Applying the concept that different people experience the same message differently.

questionBank.prompt: A video exaggerates a product's benefits, and two viewers respond. Which statement best distinguishes the skeptical stance media literacy teaches from a cynical stance?
options: Skepticism dismisses the video as worthless, while cynicism checks the claims
Skepticism assumes the creator is lying, while cynicism asks for evidence
Both stances apply identical standards of evidence
Skepticism withholds judgment and asks for evidence, while cynicism assumes deception in advance
questionBank.explanation: NAMLE describes media literacy education as developing skeptical, not cynical, approaches. Skepticism withholds judgment until evidence arrives; cynicism assumes the message is deceptive before looking, which is why the two stances produce different analyses.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the difference between skepticism and cynicism.

title: Propaganda
in30Seconds: Propaganda is deliberate, systematic communication designed to persuade an audience toward a political or ideological goal. It often presents facts selectively, uses emotionally charged language, and hides or downplays opposing information. This lesson is about recognizing propaganda, not making it: the history of the term, the classic devices identified by the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, and the questions that reveal persuasion that works by manipulation. Studying propaganda is a defense, because it sharpens judgment about who benefits from a message and what it leaves out.
whyItMatters: Propaganda does not only live in history books. Wartime posters, campaign materials, and messages circulating on social media can all use the same persuasive devices, and recognizing them changes how you read a message. Understanding propaganda also clarifies what separates it from education, news reporting, and commercial advertising, which look similar on the surface but differ in intent, transparency, and how they treat information. For citizens the practical payoff is the ability to pause, ask who benefits, notice what is missing, and decide for yourself instead of being steered. Studying propaganda is therefore a form of defense against manipulation, and the same recognition questions keep working as techniques evolve.
learningObjectives: Define propaganda as deliberate, systematic persuasion aimed at political or ideological ends, and describe the history of the term.
Distinguish propaganda from education, news reporting, advertising, and everyday persuasion using intent, transparency, and treatment of information.
Identify the seven classic devices catalogued by the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, plus loaded language, fear appeals, and repetition.
Apply recognition questions about benefit, omission, emotional manipulation, and one-sidedness to a described message.
Analyze a described message to explain how its techniques and omissions work, without reproducing or creating propaganda.

collegeVersion.heading: What propaganda is, and where the word comes from
collegeVersion.body:
Propaganda is deliberate, systematic communication intended to persuade an audience to support an agenda, most often a political or ideological one. The working definition used here has three parts: it is intentional, it is organized rather than casual, and it aims at beliefs, loyalties, or actions rather than at information alone. A propaganda message is not necessarily false, and it is not necessarily crude. It may present facts selectively, arrange them to encourage one conclusion, and use emotionally charged language that asks for a feeling rather than an examination of the evidence.

The word itself has a documented history. It comes from Modern Latin, the gerundive of propagare, meaning to spread, and its earliest institutional use belongs to the Catholic Church's Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, created in 1622 to spread the faith in non-Catholic regions. From the late eighteenth century the word also began to describe secular activities, and in the twentieth century, especially during the two world wars, it became associated with manipulation. Knowing that history matters: calling something propaganda is a modern judgment rather than a timeless label, and describing a historical campaign is not the same as endorsing it.

collegeVersion.heading: Propaganda and its neighbors: education, news, advertising, persuasion
collegeVersion.body:
Propaganda is easiest to recognize when compared with the communication forms it resembles. Education aims to build understanding; its purpose is open, and good teaching welcomes questions and corrections. News reporting aims to describe events, and its conventions include naming sources and correcting errors. Advertising aims to sell a product or service and is normally identifiable as advertising, however persuasive it is. Everyday persuasion, such as a friend urging you to see a film or a colleague arguing for a proposal, is usually open about what it wants.

Propaganda differs along three related dimensions: intent, transparency, and treatment of information. Its intent is a political or ideological goal rather than understanding or a commercial exchange. It is often not transparent: the sponsor, the purpose, or the selection of facts may be concealed. And it treats information as material to be shaped, so what is omitted is often as important as what is said. These are analytical distinctions rather than a scoring rubric: a news story can be biased and an advertisement can deceive, but each form is defined by its typical purpose and conventions. A message that hides its sponsor and stacks the evidence toward one political conclusion is best analyzed as propaganda.

collegeVersion.heading: The classic devices, catalogued by the Institute for Propaganda Analysis
collegeVersion.body:
The Institute for Propaganda Analysis, founded in 1937 by Kirtley Mather, Edward A. Filene, and Clyde R. Miller, operated until 1942 with the stated purpose of teaching people how to think rather than what to think. Its researchers catalogued seven devices that remain the standard starting list.

Name-calling attaches a negative label to a person or idea so it is dismissed without examination. Glittering generalities do the reverse: admired virtue words such as freedom or justice carry the message past scrutiny. Transfer borrows the prestige of a respected symbol, such as a flag or an institution, and lends it to the message. Testimonial enlists a respected or admired person to endorse it. Plain folks has the speaker claim to be an ordinary person like the audience. Card stacking presents only the evidence that favors one side. Bandwagon urges the audience to join because everyone else already has.

Later analyses document closely related techniques: loaded language, which uses words chosen for their emotional charge; fear appeals, which emphasize threats to push the audience toward a prescribed action; and repetition, which repeats a slogan or symbol until it feels familiar. The original list was created for recognition and defense. Using it to label a message is analysis; using it to build a message would be the very thing this lesson teaches you to recognize.

collegeVersion.heading: Recognizing propaganda: questions and two historical examples
collegeVersion.body:
Four questions turn the definition into a practical check. Who benefits if I accept this? What information is missing? Does the message lean on emotion rather than evidence? Is it one-sided, and does it say who is behind it? None of these alone proves propaganda, but together they describe how a message treats its audience.

The world wars supply the most documented examples of organized persuasion. During World War I the poster became one of the most important communication forms: the Library of Congress collection holds roughly 1,900 posters from 1914 to 1920 used to inspire, inform, and persuade, covering recruiting appeals, war-loan drives, Red Cross calls, and conservation reminders produced across many countries. During World War II the United States government ran a coordinated persuasion campaign with explicitly stated goals, recruiting professional artists and filmmakers; the National Archives exhibit Powers of Persuasion documents posters such as I Want You, by James Montgomery Flagg (Army Recruiting Bureau version, 1940), and We Can Do It!, by J. Howard Miller, produced by Westinghouse for the War Production Co-Ordinating Committee. Other governments operated official wartime information agencies, including Germany's propaganda ministry, Britain's Political Warfare Executive, and the United States Office of War Information.

These examples are described, never reproduced. The point of studying them is recognition: seeing how organized persuasion worked in the past helps you notice the same moves when they appear around you, and that defensive purpose is the ethics of this lesson.

vocabulary.definition: Deliberate, systematic communication aimed at persuading an audience to support a political or ideological agenda, often by selecting facts and using emotionally charged language.
Attaching a negative label to a person or idea so it is rejected without careful examination.

Borrowing the prestige or authority of a respected symbol and lending it to a message.
An endorsement of a message by a respected or admired person.
A speaker's claim to be an ordinary person who shares the audience's concerns.
Presenting only the evidence that supports one side of a question while ignoring the rest.
The claim that everyone is joining a cause, so the audience should join too.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Propaganda is communication made to convince you of one side, usually a political side, by leaning on feelings more than facts. It may show only the good parts, give opponents harsh labels, wrap itself in admired words like freedom, borrow the authority of a flag or a celebrity, pretend to be an ordinary neighbor, or tell you that everyone else is already on board. In the 1930s a group of researchers called the Institute for Propaganda Analysis listed seven of these tricks so that people could recognize them. Recognizing them is like learning to notice a magician's moves: you enjoy the show more, and you are much harder to trick.
eli10.analogy: Think of propaganda as a guided tour that only shows you half the building. The guide walks you through the impressive lobby, never mentions the leaky roof, and keeps saying that everyone who matters has already signed the lease. A good tour shows you the whole building, and a good message shows you the evidence on both sides.
eli10.analogyLimits: A guided tour is honest about being a tour, and you can leave any time. Propaganda often hides who is speaking and what it wants, and it can reach you through sources you already trust, which makes it harder to notice and harder to walk away from.

workedExample: Imagine a short video shared before a local election. A friendly narrator in work clothes says, 'I'm just a bus driver like you,' while a respected actor's voice praises a candidate. The word reform flashes on screen, an opponent's face appears next to the words career politician, and the closing line repeats the candidate's slogan three times. Running the recognition questions: the message hides who funded it, omits the candidate's record and the opponent's view, leans on status and emotion rather than evidence, and shows only one side. Identifying those moves is recognition, not creation. The point of this lesson is to notice such techniques, not to imitate them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating propaganda as the same thing as all persuasion or all advertising.
commonMistakes.correction: Persuasion is a broad category; propaganda is deliberate, systematic persuasion for political or ideological ends that often conceals its purpose and selects its information.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every wartime poster or official media outlet was pure manipulation.
commonMistakes.correction: Describe what a campaign did and who ran it. Historical description is not the same as endorsement, and each case needs its own evidence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the technique list as a recipe or judging a message by a single word.
commonMistakes.correction: The Institute's list was created for recognition and defense. Analyze the whole message: intent, sponsorship, omissions, and emotional appeals together.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing propaganda with news because both use media.
commonMistakes.correction: News is expected to report events, attribute sources, and correct errors; propaganda aims to advance an agenda, often without disclosing its purpose.

compareContrast.distinction: Education aims openly at understanding and is transparent about its purpose; propaganda aims to advance an agenda, often without saying so, and may select information to fit the message.
News is expected to report events, name sources, and correct errors; propaganda presents a one-sided case meant to move the audience toward a political or ideological goal.
Advertising openly seeks a commercial transaction and is usually identifiable as advertising; propaganda pursues political or ideological ends and may conceal who is behind it.

keyTakeaway: Propaganda is deliberate, systematic persuasion for political or ideological ends that often hides its purpose and shapes its information. Recognize it by asking who benefits, what is omitted, and whether emotion replaces evidence, and study it to defend against it, never to create it.

title: Media Criticism
in30Seconds: Media criticism is the practice of analyzing and evaluating media works: how they are made, what they mean, and how well they work. It differs from reviewing. A review is timely consumer guidance — should you see this now? — while criticism is sustained analysis of meaning and value. Critics describe what they observe, analyze how the parts relate, interpret what the work says, and evaluate it with reasons. Strong criticism is an argued judgment, not a verdict, and it is only as good as its evidence.
whyItMatters: Criticism sharpens how we consume media. It gives us vocabulary for describing what a film or series does, questions for examining craft and meaning, and reasons for preferring one work over another. It also makes us better readers of reviews, ratings, and online hot takes: we can tell when a claim is supported by evidence and when it is merely taste dressed up as fact. Because critics help guide attention and public debate, understanding their practice improves our own judgment — whether we are writing an essay about a film, discussing a show with friends, or deciding which critical voices to trust. The habit of describing, analyzing, interpreting, and evaluating with reasons transfers to every medium we encounter.
learningObjectives: Define media criticism as sustained analysis and evaluation of a work's meaning, form, and value.
Distinguish criticism from review by purpose, timing, and audience.
Identify the objects of criticism: formal craft, narrative, representation, ideology, and audience effects.
Name and attribute the major critical approaches: formalist, ideological, feminist, and audience-oriented.
Apply a description-analysis-interpretation-evaluation method to a described media work.
Evaluate a critical claim's fairness, evidence, and disclosed conflicts of interest.

collegeVersion.heading: Criticism and review are different practices
collegeVersion.body: Media criticism is the sustained study, interpretation, and evaluation of a media work: what it means, how its structure and style produce that meaning, and how it compares with other works in its genre or history. The University of Vermont's film-studies guide describes criticism as offering interpretation of meaning, analysis of structure and style, judgment of worth by comparison with other films, and an estimation of likely effect on viewers. A movie review, by contrast, is consumer-oriented. Published around a film's release, it emphasizes recommendation over analysis: it explains the premise, weighs merits and flaws, and often ends in a star rating. Criticism may appear years after a release and is usually longer and more complex. Reviews can contain real analysis, and criticism often reaches a verdict, but their jobs differ. A review answers, "Should you spend your evening on this now?" Criticism asks, "How does this work, and what is it worth?"

collegeVersion.heading: What critics examine
collegeVersion.body: Good criticism says which object it is addressing. Formal craft covers how cinematography, editing, sound, performance, and design shape the work; MIT's viewing guide offers a checklist — camera distance and movement, editing and transitions, lighting, mise-en-scène, sound, storytelling — as a starting inventory. Narrative concerns how a work organizes and discloses story information. Representation concerns how a work portrays groups, identities, and social roles. Ideology concerns the values, assumptions, and power relations embedded in the work; media messages can range from overt statements to vague expressions of cultural values, and cultures are not monolithic. Audience effects concern what a work might do for or to viewers — a question researchers genuinely disagree about. Keeping these objects separate keeps claims honest: a statement about editing is not automatically a statement about ideology, and a claim about a work's values is not a claim about what viewers actually felt.

collegeVersion.heading: Frameworks critics use
collegeVersion.body: Formalist criticism attends closely to form and craft — how images, editing, and structure create meaning. Its roots run deep: André Bazin and the writers of Cahiers du Cinéma, including later directors François Truffaut and Jean-Luc Godard, and, in later academic film studies, David Bordwell and Kristin Thompson. Ideological criticism examines the values and power relations embedded in a work and asks whose interests its worldview serves. Such readings are contested: some critics praised Birth of a Nation's narrative complexity while others were outraged by its openly racist attitudes, and some critics have labeled strongly argued documentaries propagandistic. Feminist criticism, informed by feminist film theory, asks how a work represents gender and what assumptions about viewers it carries. Audience-oriented criticism studies how viewers interpret and respond to works; it reflects research that audiences are not passive — the direct-effects model of the 1920s and 1930s was challenged by studies such as the 1940 People's Choice research. These are lenses, not verdicts: a framework explains the questions a critic asks, not the answers.

collegeVersion.heading: The critic's toolkit: a four-stage method
collegeVersion.body: Description reports what is observable: the shots, cuts, sounds, and events, stated as neutrally as possible. Analysis identifies how the parts relate: how shot lengths interact, how a sound bridges a cut, how a scene answers a question the opening raised. Interpretation proposes what the work means — what its patterns suggest about its subject, characters, or world. Evaluation judges the work with reasons: whether the choices serve the meaning described, and how the work compares with others like it. These stages mirror the guide's four components: interpretation of meaning, analysis of structure and style, judgment of worth, and estimation of effect on viewers. Consider an invented short film, Northbound, about a night-shift courier. The critic notes the long takes and the recurring radio static (description); observes that every cut away from the courier lands on a phone notification (analysis); argues the film treats waiting as labor (interpretation); and judges that the restraint suits the theme, though the final scene under-explains the choice (evaluation). Each stage must be checkable: another viewer should be able to confirm the description while still disagreeing with the evaluation.

collegeVersion.heading: The role and limits of criticism
collegeVersion.body: Critics guide attention and debate. Reviews appear before most people have seen a film, and research finds that critics' judgments can influence a film's early box-office performance. But criticism does not control outcomes: films that receive a lousy critical reception can still do extremely well when marketing creates enough hype. Its limits follow from its nature. Taste is not universal, and a critic's judgment is shaped by values, experience, and context. Two thoughtful critics can disagree about the same pacing without either lacking evidence. Criticism is best treated as an invitation to think, not a final verdict.

collegeVersion.heading: The ethics of criticism
collegeVersion.body: Because criticism is argument, its ethics are the ethics of honest argument. The Society of Professional Journalists organizes professional ethics around four principles: seek truth and report it, minimize harm, act independently, and be accountable. For a critic these become practical duties. Fairness means representing the work accurately — describing what is actually on screen, not what you assumed — and engaging the strongest version of what the work attempts. Independence means disclosing conflicts: if you worked on the film, if the studio advertises in your outlet, or if you are close to the director, say so, because an undisclosed relationship makes judgment suspect. Accountability means standing behind your reasons and correcting errors. A critic who engages the work honestly can be wrong; a critic who engages something else — a disliked genre, an imagined audience, a grudge — has stopped doing criticism.

vocabulary.definition: The sustained analysis and evaluation of a media work's meaning, form, and value, argued with evidence rather than delivered as a verdict.
Timely, consumer-oriented writing about a new release that weighs a work's merits and flaws to help readers decide whether to see it.
The stage of criticism that identifies how a work's parts relate, such as how shots, sounds, and scenes connect.
A reasoned proposal about what a work means, based on its observable patterns and its context.
A judged assessment of a work's worth, supported by reasons and by comparison with similar works.
An approach that examines how a work's form and craft — images, editing, sound, structure — create meaning.
An approach that examines the values, assumptions, and power relations embedded in a media work.
An approach informed by feminist theory that asks how a work represents gender and what assumptions about viewers it carries.
An approach that studies how viewers interpret, respond to, and make use of media works.
A personal or professional relationship that could unfairly influence a critic's judgment and should be disclosed.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Media criticism is thinking carefully about a movie or show and explaining your thinking. You look at what you actually see and hear, notice how the pieces fit together, say what you think it means, and then say whether it works — with reasons. A review tells people whether a new film is worth seeing this week. Criticism digs deeper and can happen any time, about anything on screen. You do not need to be an expert to start; you need to pay attention, take notes, and be willing to change your mind when the evidence points elsewhere.
eli10.analogy: Think of two guides at a museum. One stands at the entrance of a new exhibition and tells visitors whether it is worth their ticket — that is a reviewer. The other walks with you through the rooms, points out how the lighting shapes each piece, connects the pieces to each other and to the artist's other work, and explains what the exhibition is trying to do — that is a critic. Both are useful; they are doing different jobs.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy has limits. Media works are watched over time, with sound, editing, and narrative, not hung in rooms. And a film critic's walk-through is written in words, so critics must choose what to describe and may miss what matters to you. Criticism is one careful reading, never the only one.

workedExample: Invented example: The Last Bus, a 98-minute drama about a night bus driver. A critic applies the four-stage method. Description: the film holds long takes of the empty bus, the driver's radio crackles between stops, and there is no music. Analysis: every time the driver reaches for the radio, the film cuts to a passenger's face, and the pattern repeats each night of the week shown. Interpretation: the film suggests that connection on a night shift is fragile and mostly imagined. Evaluation: the restraint serves the loneliness at the film's center, though the final scene, in which the driver resigns without explanation, asks more of viewers than the earlier pattern prepares them for. Each claim can be checked against the film itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling any piece of writing about media "criticism" when it is actually a review.
commonMistakes.correction: Check the job: a review is timely consumer guidance; criticism is sustained analysis of meaning and value. The same person can write both.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping description and jumping straight to a verdict.
commonMistakes.correction: State what is observable first. A judgment without a checkable description is an opinion without evidence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating personal dislike as analysis.
commonMistakes.correction: Dislike is a starting point, not an argument. Identify what the work does and why you respond that way before evaluating it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating disagreement with a critic as proof that the critic is wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: Criticism is argued interpretation; two critics can observe the same pacing and evaluate it differently. Assess the reasons, not just the conclusion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming claims about ideology or audience effects are facts about the work or its viewers.
commonMistakes.correction: Ideological readings are interpretations, and effects claims are contested. Attribute them as such and keep them separate from what is observable.

compareContrast.distinction: Criticism offers sustained analysis of meaning and value and can appear any time; a review is timely consumer guidance around a release, emphasizing recommendation over analysis.
Analysis explains how parts of a work relate; interpretation proposes what the work means, building on that analysis.
Formalist criticism examines how form and craft create meaning; ideological criticism examines the values and power relations embedded in a work.

keyTakeaway: Media criticism is argued analysis of meaning and value: describe what is observable, analyze how parts relate, interpret what the work means, and evaluate with reasons — honestly, and with conflicts disclosed.

title: Teach Descriptively And Comparatively, Not Devotionally.
in30Seconds: Teach Descriptively And Comparatively, Not Devotionally. is a foundational concept in Religious Studies. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.
whyItMatters: College courses use teach descriptively and comparatively, not devotionally. as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions.
learningObjectives: Define teach descriptively and comparatively, not devotionally. using course-appropriate language.
Identify important features and limits of teach descriptively and comparatively, not devotionally..
Apply teach descriptively and comparatively, not devotionally. to a simple scenario.

collegeVersion.heading: The core idea
collegeVersion.body: Teach Descriptively And Comparatively, Not Devotionally. is a concept students use to organize information, ask better questions, and explain relationships in Religious Studies. A college-level explanation names the concept, describes its parts, and shows how those parts work together. title: What Is Religion?
in30Seconds: In Religious Studies, religion is a category for investigating human beliefs, practices, communities, values, and orientations to what people regard as sacred or ultimate. Scholars do not use one universally accepted definition. Instead, a definition makes its focus and boundaries visible. Some definitions ask what a tradition is about; others ask what roles it plays in personal or social life.
whyItMatters: A definition determines what a question can notice. It can affect which practices, communities, and historical cases a researcher includes, compares, or leaves at the edge of a study. Learning to name a definition’s purpose and limits helps students read claims about religion more carefully. It also supports accurate comparison: traditions should not be judged by whether they resemble one familiar example.
learningObjectives: Define religion as a contested analytical category in Religious Studies.
Distinguish substantive and functional approaches to defining religion.
Explain how a definition’s boundaries shape a comparison.
Apply a stated definition cautiously to a new example.
Analyze why a single checklist can produce difficult boundary cases.

collegeVersion.heading: A category, not a final answer
collegeVersion.body:
The ordinary question "What is religion?" sounds as if it should have one short, final answer. In Religious Studies, it is more productive to begin with a different question: what work is a particular definition meant to do? A definition is a rule for grouping cases together. It highlights some features and makes other features less central. That is useful, but it means a definition is never neutral in its consequences. A definition centered on devotion to gods, for example, will sort cases differently from one centered on ritual, community, moral order, or a relationship to what participants regard as sacred.

Scholars therefore treat religion as a contested category rather than assuming that every tradition shares one necessary feature. The contest is not merely a vocabulary dispute. It concerns the evidence a scholar will examine and the comparisons a scholar can responsibly make. A narrow definition may make a study precise, while also creating exclusions that must be acknowledged. A broad definition may notice more similarities, while also risking that many unrelated activities appear to belong together. Good academic work names its working definition and remains alert to cases that strain it.

This approach does not ask students to decide whether a religion is true, false, valuable, or invalid. It asks them to describe how people, communities, texts, practices, and institutions are organized and interpreted. A student can recognize that a participant calls a place sacred without making a personal claim about the place. That distinction makes comparative study possible while respecting that traditions are lived in diverse ways.

collegeVersion.heading: Substantive and functional approaches
collegeVersion.body:
One major family of definitions is substantive. A substantive approach identifies the kind of reality, being, or domain to which religion is oriented. Depending on the scholar, that focus may be gods, spirits, the sacred, transcendence, or an unseen order. These definitions can help distinguish religious claims from other kinds of claims, because they specify an object or orientation. They may, however, fit some traditions better than others. If a definition requires belief in a deity, it can make non-theistic traditions hard to describe even when those traditions contain disciplined practices, ethical teachings, institutions, and inherited ways of interpreting life.

A functional approach instead emphasizes what religious ideas and practices do. Researchers using this approach may examine how a tradition creates solidarity, provides meaning, marks life transitions, organizes moral commitments, or shapes identity. OpenStax’s sociological overview presents religion as both personal and social, drawing attention to beliefs, practices, norms, and group life. Functional approaches make those observable roles easier to study. Yet they can become so broad that activities not ordinarily identified as religious are included because they also create identity or cohesion.

Neither approach automatically wins. They answer different questions and create different boundary lines. Some scholars combine substantive and functional criteria; others use a family-resemblance approach, looking for overlapping features rather than a single required trait. The key skill is not memorizing a winner. It is asking what a definition includes, what it excludes, and whether those results fit the purpose of the inquiry.

collegeVersion.heading: Using definitions carefully in comparison
collegeVersion.body:
A careful comparison begins by stating the lens. Suppose a researcher is comparing a weekly gathering, a memorial practice, and a text-centered study group. A functional lens might ask whether each activity builds community, offers a shared account of suffering, or marks a transition. A substantive lens might ask whether participants relate the activity to a sacred or transcendent reality. Neither question alone settles whether each case is religion. Instead, the answers show how the classification depends on the stated rule.

The evidence should be more specific than a label. Researchers can attend to participants’ own descriptions, rituals, narratives, material objects, ethical commitments, organizations, and historical setting. They should also avoid treating a named tradition as internally uniform. Members may disagree about beliefs, change practices over time, or describe the same activity differently. A classification can be useful while still being provisional: "under this definition, these features support comparison; under another definition, the boundary may move."

This discipline prevents two common errors. One is essentialism: reducing a large, changing tradition to one supposed core feature. The other is overextension: calling any intense commitment a religion without explaining why. In introductory study, the most defensible conclusion is often conditional rather than absolute. State the definition, show the relevant evidence, identify a limit, and leave room for a revised account when better evidence or a different research question calls for one.

vocabulary.definition: A contested category used to study certain systems of meaning, practice, community, and orientation.
A stated rule that identifies what a concept includes and excludes for a purpose.

An approach that emphasizes the social or personal roles beliefs and practices may perform.
Set apart as specially meaningful, worthy of reverence, or connected to a religious orientation.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine several boxes of things from different neighborhoods: a songbook, a special meal, a quiet meditation practice, a building where people gather, and a story about where the world came from. You might notice that some belong together, but no single item is in every box. Scholars face a similar problem when they use the word religion. They make a rule for a question, explain the rule, and check whether it treats different communities fairly. The rule is a tool for studying; it is not a test that tells people what they must believe.
eli10.analogy: A definition is like a map key. A map key tells you what the symbols mean so you can follow a route. A substantive key might mark places connected to the sacred. A functional key might mark places or practices that help a group make meaning or hold together. Different keys reveal different parts of the same landscape.
eli10.analogyLimits: Unlike map symbols, human traditions change, overlap, and are described differently by participants. A definition cannot capture every lived detail, so a researcher must explain its limits.

workedExample: A class compares two memorial gatherings. In the first, participants recite inherited words, light candles, and describe the gathering as an encounter with the sacred. In the second, participants share stories and support one another but do not connect the event to a sacred reality. A substantive definition may include the first more readily. A functional definition may find that both help participants make meaning and strengthen relationships. The responsible conclusion is not that one label is permanently correct. The student should state which definition is being used, identify the evidence, and note how a different definition changes the result.
